cards.label: einops rearrange
cards.title: Relabel the shelves, never the jars

1.plain: Name the axes on both sides of an arrow and einops works out the transpose/reshape for you.
1.pic: A tensor is a pantry of jars on numbered shelves; rearrange rewrites the shelf labels and walks the jars into the new layout, but never opens a jar.

2.what: A way to change a tensor's layout by naming its axes instead of numbering them.
2.when: Whenever you permute, flatten, split or merge axes, which is most days in ML code.
2.why: Names make intent checkable, so shape-compatible mistakes stop being silent.

where: Splitting and merging attention heads in every transformer
Patches in vision transformers: 'b c (h p1) (w p2) -> b (h w) (p1 p2 c)'
Reading and writing activation caches by named axis in TransformerLens

cards.label: einops reduce
cards.title: Cross off a label, pour the shelf

1.plain: A named-axis mean/sum/max: the axes you drop from the right-hand side are the ones reduced over.
1.pic: A tensor is a pantry of jars on labelled shelves; reduce is a new floor plan with a label crossed off, so every jar along that shelf is poured together into one, and the last word on the plan says how to pour.

2.what: A named-axis mean, sum or max: the axes missing from the output are the ones collapsed.
2.when: Whenever you pool an image, average a loss, or summarise activations across a batch.
2.why: Naming the collapsed axis makes the reduction readable and checkable, and since it cannot be undone you want it right first time.

where: Global average pooling at the end of every ResNet: 'b c h w -> b c', 'mean'
Max pooling as one reduce over (h h2) (w w2)
Averaging a loss over batch and sequence positions
Mean activations over a dataset, the baseline for mean-ablation and steering

cards.label: einsum
cards.title: The one-line tensor contract

1.plain: Write the index letters of both inputs and the output; repeated letters are summed over.
1.pic: einsum is like a one-line contract at a notary's office: each tensor signs with its axis letters, letters written after the arrow are kept, and letters left off are multiplied together and summed away.

2.what: A one-line way to multiply and sum tensors by naming every axis with a letter.
2.when: Whenever you would otherwise chain transposes, matmuls and sums, most of all for attention scores.
2.why: The letters say exactly which axes are matched, kept and summed, so your intent is readable and checkable in one place.

where: Attention scores in one line: einsum('bqhd,bkhd->bhqk', q, k)
Convolution, written as a multiply-and-sum over each window
Batched ray-object intersection in [0.1]
Reading mech-interp papers, which write weight products and contractions as einsums

cards.label: Broadcasting
cards.title: Line up right, mirror the ones

1.plain: Trailing dimensions of size 1 are stretched to match; anything else is an error.
1.pic: Broadcasting is two dance troupes pairing up one to one: they line up from the right, a troupe with a lone dancer on a line stands before a mirror and is seen as many times as needed, and if both have several dancers but different counts the show stops.

2.what: The rule that lets tensors of different shapes combine, by lining shapes up from the right and stretching size-1 axes.
2.when: Every elementwise operation between tensors whose shapes are not identical, which is most lines of tensor code.
2.why: It saves copies and loops, but it also makes the commonest shape mistake legal, so the habit that matters is asserting the shape you meant.

where: Adding a bias vector to every row of a batch
Unbroadcast in backprop: the gradient sums the stretched copies back down
Batched ray tracing in [0.1]: many rays tested in one expression
sum(dim=1) without keepdim=True, then dividing: the sums line up as a row, not a column

cards.label: Batched raytracing
cards.title: A clerk at every desk

1.plain: Do every ray against every triangle at once by adding batch axes instead of writing a loop.
1.pic: Batched raytracing is like an exam hall with a desk for every (ray, triangle) pair, rays down the side and triangles along the top, because every pair needs the same small worksheet and all of them can be written at the same moment.

2.what: Testing every ray against every triangle in one tensor operation, by giving each list its own axis of a shared table.
2.when: Whenever you catch yourself writing a nested loop that does the same small calculation for every pair from two lists.
2.why: One batched call keeps the GPU busy instead of paying Python overhead per pair, and a written shape chain makes the plan checkable before it runs.

where: Attention scores: every query against every key in one (q, k) table
Pairwise distances, such as every point against every cluster centre
Running a whole batch of prompts through a model in one forward pass

steps.checkpoint: Write a rearrange pattern that turns (batch, channel, height, width) into a single stacked image grid, from memory, in under two minutes.
three: The size-2 and size-3 axes look identical. (NR, 2, 3) has a points axis and a dims axis, and unbind, stack and indexing will all happily take the wrong one. Before any of those calls, say the axis name out loud, not its number.

Broadcasting does not fail loudly. A missing keepdim=True, or a (m,) where you meant (m, 1), produces a legal result of the wrong shape whenever two of your sizes coincide — and in small test cases they usually do.

The line that errors is rarely the line that is wrong. A bad dim= on a stack surfaces at the det two lines later. Fix this by annotating shapes as you write, not by reading backwards from the traceback.

cards.label: Convolution
cards.title: One stencil, slid everywhere

1.plain: Slide one small weight tensor over the input and take a dot product at every position.
1.pic: A convolution is like sliding one small stencil across a photo and scoring, at every spot, how well the patch underneath matches it; because the same stencil is reused everywhere, it needs few weights and only ever looks at neighbours.

2.what: Sliding one small learned grid of weights across an input and taking a dot product at every position.
2.when: Whenever the input has spatial structure, where nearby values belong together, as in photographs.
2.why: Reusing one kernel everywhere means far fewer weights and a built-in assumption of locality, which is how AlexNet beat a decade of hand-built features.

where: Every vision network since AlexNet, ResNet included
Max pooling: the same sliding window and size formula, with no learned weights
Transposed convolutions in a GAN generator, doubling the size instead of halving it
The edge and curve detectors interpretability finds in early vision layers

cards.label: Linear layer
cards.title: A mixing desk of learned faders

1.plain: A learned matrix multiply plus a bias; the unit every other module is assembled from.
1.pic: A linear layer is a mixing desk: each output speaker plays its own blend of every input channel, set by a row of faders plus one offset knob, and training is an engineer nudging those faders until the mix sounds right.

2.what: A learned matrix multiply plus a bias: every output is a weighted blend of every input, plus an offset.
2.when: Whenever a model needs to mix features into new ones, which is almost every learnable step in an MLP or a transformer.
2.why: It is the simplest map that lets every output depend on every input with a learnable strength, and because it is linear it is the part of a model you can read most directly.

where: The query, key, value and output projections inside every attention head
A linear probe: one linear layer trained on frozen activations to read a concept
LoRA: a thin pair of linear maps added beside a frozen weight
The unembedding: a linear map from the residual stream to one logit per token

cards.label: BatchNorm2d
cards.title: Grade the class, remember the curve

1.plain: Normalise each channel over the batch during training, then use running statistics at eval time.
1.pic: BatchNorm is like a teacher who curves each exam question against today's class and jots the class average in a notebook, so a student sitting a make-up exam alone can be graded from the notebook instead.

2.what: A layer that normalises each channel using the current batch's statistics during training and remembered running averages at evaluation.
2.when: In CNNs such as ResNets, typically between a convolution and its ReLU; transformers use LayerNorm instead.
2.why: It keeps activations in a sane range so deep networks train faster and care less about initialisation, but its batch dependence makes the train/eval switch mandatory.

where: Dropout, the other common layer that behaves differently under model.train() and model.eval()
LayerNorm in every transformer: the same normalise-then-rescale, pooled inside one example
Any buffer: state that must travel with a checkpoint but must never be trained
3.judge: Ioffe and Szegedy (2015) credited 'internal covariate shift'. Santurkar et al. (NeurIPS 2018) injected shifting noise after BatchNorm and it still beat no normalisation. Their account: a smoother loss landscape.

cards.label: Residual block
cards.title: Pencil notes, never retype the page

1.plain: Add the block's input to its output so gradients have a path that skips the block entirely.
1.pic: A residual block is like an editor who pencils notes onto the page and passes page plus notes along, instead of retyping the whole thing; with nothing to add, the page goes through untouched.

2.what: A block that learns a correction F(x) and adds it to its own input, so it outputs x + F(x).
2.when: Whenever you stack many layers: ResNets for images, and the residual stream of every transformer.
2.why: Doing nothing becomes the easy default and gradients get a direct path back, so very deep networks actually train.

where: The transformer residual stream: every attention head and MLP adds its output to one running sum
Zero-ablating a block in interpretability: the stream survives because the block only ever added to it
LoRA fine-tuning: learn a small update added to frozen weights, starting from zero

cards.label: SGD
cards.title: Feel the slope, take a stride

1.plain: Step downhill: subtract the learning rate times the gradient.
1.pic: SGD is like walking down a hillside in thick fog: you cannot see the valley, so you feel which way the ground rises under your boots and take one stride the other way, again and again.

2.what: The basic learning step: move every weight a little in the direction that lowers the loss, scaled by the learning rate.
2.when: On every training step of every network you train, either directly or inside a fancier optimiser like Adam.
2.why: The gradient only tells you which way is downhill right here, so small steps trust that local reading only as far as it stays true.

where: Every optimiser you will use (momentum, RMSprop, Adam, AdamW) is this step plus a correction
Fine-tuning, RLHF and SAE training all run the same loop: compute a loss, step against its gradient
Fitting any curve by nudging its knobs against the error, from a straight-line fit to a frontier model

cards.label: Momentum
cards.title: The heavy ball in the ravine

1.plain: Keep a running average of past gradients and step along that instead, so consistent directions accumulate.
1.pic: Momentum is a heavy ball rolling down a narrow ravine: each gradient is a shove, the ball's velocity remembers past shoves, so shoves that keep agreeing (along the valley) pile up while shoves that flip side to side (across it) cancel.

2.what: Step along a decaying running sum of past gradients instead of the latest gradient alone.
2.when: Whenever the loss surface is a narrow valley or the gradients are noisy, which is nearly always; in practice it arrives built into Adam.
2.why: Directions that agree step after step get amplified and directions that flip get damped, so the optimiser rolls along the valley instead of rattling across it.

where: Adam and AdamW: the first moment is a momentum-style running average of gradients
BatchNorm's running mean and variance: decay the old, add the new (PyTorch even names the knob momentum)
Any noisy signal you smooth with an exponential moving average, from loss curves to metrics

cards.label: Adam
cards.title: Every weight gets its own ruler

1.plain: Keep a running mean and a running variance per parameter and step by mean over root-variance, so every parameter gets its own effective learning rate.
1.pic: Adam is like handing every weight its own ruler: it keeps a running average of each weight's slope and of how big that slope usually is, then measures the slope in its own ruler's units, so busy and quiet weights both take sensible steps.

2.what: An optimiser that steps each weight by its averaged gradient divided by the root of its averaged squared gradient.
2.when: Almost every time you train a network in this course, usually in its AdamW form.
2.why: Dividing by each weight's own typical gradient size gives every parameter a sensible step at once, where a single learning rate is too big for some weights and too small for others.

where: AdamW, the default optimiser for every transformer you train in later chapters
Momentum and RMSprop, Adam's two halves, each still used on its own
Running averages elsewhere: BatchNorm keeps the same kind of slowly updated statistics

cards.label: Weight decay
cards.title: A rubber band back to zero

1.plain: Shrink every weight a little each step; an L2 penalty applied by the optimiser rather than the loss.
1.pic: Weight decay is like tying every weight to zero with a weak rubber band: the data drags each weight out to where it is useful, the band tugs it back in proportion to how far it has gone, and the weight rests where the two pulls balance.

2.what: A steady pull of every weight towards zero, applied by the optimiser at each step.
2.when: On almost every training run, as AdamW's weight_decay setting, applied to weights but not to biases or norm scales.
2.why: It keeps each weight only as big as the data keeps paying for, so the model cannot lean on a few huge weights.

where: Ridge regression: the same L2 pull in classic statistics
The KL penalty in RLHF: a leash back to a reference model instead of back to zero
Every AdamW run you launch has this knob

cards.label: Computational graph
cards.title: Every bowl remembers its recipe

1.plain: The forward pass records which tensors made which, so the backward pass has a route to walk.
1.pic: A computational graph is a kitchen where every bowl gets a card taped on saying which recipe made it and which bowls went in, so when the dish tastes wrong you can follow the cards back and share out the blame.

2.what: A record, made during the forward pass, of which operation produced each tensor and from which parents.
2.when: Every time you compute from tensors that need gradients, which is every training step.
2.why: Backprop needs a route from the loss back to every weight, and recording it as you go gets every gradient in one backward sweep instead of one run per weight.

where: loss.backward() in every PyTorch training loop
Spreadsheets tracking which cells depend on which, so they recalculate in the right order
Build tools like make, which record what each file was built from
Gradient-based attribution in interpretability, walking back from an output to inner activations

cards.label: Backward function
cards.title: An exchange booth at every step

1.plain: Each op stores how to turn 'gradient w.r.t. my output' into 'gradient w.r.t. each of my inputs'.
1.pic: A backward function is like an exchange booth at each step of a road: blame for the result arrives in the output's currency, and the booth converts it at its own local rate into blame for each of its inputs.

2.what: A small rule stored with each operation that turns the loss's sensitivity to its output into sensitivity to each of its inputs.
2.when: Every time you call loss.backward(), and whenever you write a custom operation or debug a gradient that is too big, too small or the wrong shape.
2.why: It turns one global question, which knobs matter, into many tiny local ones that each operation can answer on its own.

where: loss.backward() in every training loop: PyTorch runs one of these per operation, in reverse order
Attribution methods in interpretability, which read gradients with respect to activations
Any chain of conversions where rates multiply: currencies, gear trains, unit conversions

cards.label: Backprop & topological order
cards.title: Pass the blame back, add it up

1.plain: Walk the graph in reverse topological order, applying each backward function and summing where a tensor was used more than once.
1.pic: Backprop is a kitchen inquest run backwards from the judge's score: each cook waits until every dish they fed into has sent back a note saying how much the score moves per unit of their ingredient, adds those notes up, and only then sends notes on to their own suppliers.

2.what: Getting every weight's gradient in one backward sweep, walking the graph from the loss outwards so each node's incoming gradient is complete, and adding where a value was used twice.
2.when: Every time you call loss.backward(); you build it by hand once in [0.4], then let autograd do it forever after.
2.why: Nudging each weight and re-running the model needs one full run per weight; backprop gets them all from one forward and one backward pass.

where: loss.backward() in every training loop: this exact walk, done for you by autograd
Build systems and spreadsheets: compute a cell only once everything it depends on is ready
Gradient-based attribution in interpretability: the same backward walk from a logit to an activation

cards.label: Cross-entropy loss
cards.title: A surprise bill for every bet

1.plain: Negative log-probability of the correct token, computed straight from logits for numerical stability.
1.pic: Cross-entropy is like a bettor spreading chips across every horse and then paying a bill of -log(share of chips on the winner): all chips on the winner costs nothing, a thin share costs a lot, and none at all is unpayable.

2.what: The average of -log(probability the model gave the right answer), computed straight from the logits.
2.when: Whenever a model outputs a distribution over classes or tokens and you train or measure it, which is every language model.
2.why: It punishes confident mistakes hardest, has the clean gradient 'predicted minus true', and read per token it doubles as a probe of what the model knows.

where: Training every classifier and language model, from MNIST in [0.2] to your transformer in [1.1]
Per-token loss on a repeated random sequence: the induction-head signature in [1.2]
Perplexity, which is e raised to the average cross-entropy
Distillation, where the target is a teacher's whole distribution instead of one right answer

cards.label: Autoencoder
cards.title: A telegram with a word limit

1.plain: Squeeze the input through a narrow bottleneck and reconstruct it; the bottleneck is forced to be a compressed code.
1.pic: An autoencoder is like a sender and a receiver who may pass only a five-word telegram: to let the receiver redraw the picture, they invent a private shorthand that keeps only what matters.

2.what: A network trained to rebuild its own input through a narrow middle layer, which forces that layer to become a compressed code.
2.when: When you want a compact representation without labels, or as the starting shape for VAEs and sparse autoencoders.
2.why: Rebuilding through a bottleneck means the code has to keep what matters most about the input and drop the rest.

where: VAEs and GANs, which turn the decoder half into a generator
Sparse autoencoders on model activations: the same encode-and-rebuild, but wider and sparse
Transcoders: the same shape trained to rebuild an MLP's output from its input
Compression in general: a code is good if the receiver can rebuild the message from it

cards.label: Latent space
cards.title: A map the model draws itself

1.plain: The coordinates the bottleneck learns; interpolating between two of them should give plausible outputs.
1.pic: A latent space is a map the model draws for itself: a clerk writes down each picture's address, a painter paints whatever lives at an address, and the map is only useful if nearby addresses paint similar pictures and there are no blank streets in between.

2.what: The small coordinate space an encoder maps inputs into, where position is supposed to mean something.
2.when: Whenever a model compresses inputs through a bottleneck and you want to sample from it, interpolate in it or read what it learned.
2.why: A latent space is only useful if nearby points mean similar things and the gaps decode sensibly, which a plain autoencoder never guarantees and a VAE forces.

where: GANs also generate from a latent, reached by a completely different route
The residual stream: interpretability reads activations as a space with meaningful directions
Sparse autoencoders learn a dictionary of latents for a model's activations
The reparameterisation trick recurs wherever a model has to sample and still be differentiable

cards.label: KL divergence
cards.title: The extra surprise tax

1.plain: How far one distribution is from another, in nats; zero only when they are identical.
1.pic: KL divergence is the extra surprise tax you pay, on average, for packing by a wrong forecast Q while the weather really follows P: zero only if the forecast is perfect, and ruinous if it calls real weather impossible.

2.what: A number, in nats, for the extra surprise you pay on average by expecting Q when outcomes really follow P.
2.when: Whenever one distribution must be compared with or held close to another: a prior, a frozen base model, the same model before an intervention.
2.why: It is zero only when the two match and punishes calling real outcomes near-impossible, which is exactly the drift you want to catch.

where: The VAE loss, keeping each input's latent cloud close to a standard normal prior
The RLHF and GRPO penalty, holding a fine-tuned policy near a frozen reference model
Measuring how much an intervention changed a model's output distribution
Cross-entropy training: against fixed labels, minimising cross-entropy minimises KL, since the entropy part never moves

three: Per-channel vectors do not broadcast with feature maps. Anything of shape (C,) — a batchnorm mean, variance, weight or bias — must be reshaped to (1, C, 1, 1) before it meets a (b, C, H, W) tensor.

In-place versus rebinding. theta -= lr*g and b.copy_(...), never theta = theta - ... or b = .... Symptom is a flat loss with no error. If your partner's loss will not move, this is the first thing to check — it is the single most common bug in this whole day.

The return shape is the input's shape, not the output's. When a backward function returns something the wrong size, the answer is almost always a missing unbroadcast (elementwise ops), a missing expand_dims (sum), or a missing transpose (matmul).

cards.label: Tokenization
cards.title: Print with the stamps you have

1.plain: Text becomes integer ids from a fixed vocabulary, and the split is rarely where you'd put it.
1.pic: Tokenizing is printing text with a fixed box of rubber stamps: common chunks have their own numbered stamp, rare words are spelled from several small ones, and the space before a word is carved onto the same stamp.

2.what: Turning text into a sequence of integer ids from a fixed vocabulary of chunks, built by repeatedly merging frequent pairs.
2.when: Every time text goes into or comes out of a language model, and first thing in every interpretability experiment.
2.why: The model never sees letters, only chunks, so where the cuts fall and whether a space is attached decide what you are actually measuring.

where: Prompt templates: one stray trailing space changes the tokens the model sees
Arithmetic and spelling slips: the model sees chunks, not digits or letters
Interpretability: every logit difference and patch position is keyed to a token
Glitch tokens like ' SolidGoldMagikarp': vocabulary slots the model never learned

cards.label: Embedding
cards.title: The number only opens a locker

1.plain: A lookup table turning each token id into a vector in the residual stream.
1.pic: An embedding is a wall of numbered lockers: a token id is just a locker number, and what the model actually computes with is the learned list of numbers kept inside that locker.

2.what: A learned table with one vector per token id; embedding a token means reading its row.
2.when: At the very start of every transformer forward pass; you implement Embed once in [1.1], then it is nn.Embedding.
2.why: Token ids are arbitrary labels, so a learned vector per id gives the model something it can compute with, and it is where the residual stream begins.

where: Positional embeddings: the same lookup, keyed by position instead of token
Recommender systems: one learned vector per user and per item
The unembedding W_U: the trip back, from the residual stream to a score for every token

cards.label: Positional embedding
cards.title: Every seat tints whoever sits there

1.plain: A learned vector added per position, because attention itself has no notion of order.
1.pic: Attention is a table where every word can look at every other word at once, but nobody has a seat number; a positional embedding hangs a learned coloured lamp over each seat, and whoever sits there takes on its tint, so the others can tell where each word sat.

2.what: A learned vector for each position, added to each token's embedding so the model knows where every word sits.
2.when: At the very start of every forward pass, and again with care whenever you generate with a KV cache.
2.why: Attention compares only contents, so without position the model could not tell dog bites man from man bites dog.

where: Previous-token heads, which look one step back using positional embeddings alone
Induction heads, built on previous-token heads through K-composition
KV caching, where the position index must continue from the cached length
RoPE in newer models such as the [4.3] reasoning model: position by rotating queries and keys

cards.label: LayerNorm
cards.title: Auto-exposure for every token

1.plain: Centre and rescale each token's residual vector, then apply a learned gain and bias.
1.pic: LayerNorm is like auto-exposure on every photo: each token's vector has its own average brightness subtracted and its contrast set to a standard, then the studio's fixed colour grade is applied, so a dark shot and a bright shot of the same scene come out the same.

2.what: A per-token reset that shifts each residual vector to mean zero and unit spread, then applies a learned gain and bias.
2.when: Before every attention and MLP sublayer, and before the unembedding, in GPT-style transformers.
2.why: It keeps every layer's input in a sane range whatever earlier layers added, which steadies training; its input-dependent scale is why interpretability tools must fold or freeze it.

where: BatchNorm in the [0.2] ResNet: the same shift and scale, but per feature across the batch, with train and eval modes
TransformerLens's fold_ln, and the scale factor you apply by hand in direct logit attribution
RMSNorm in newer models, which skips the centring and divides by the root-mean-square
Cosine similarity, which also keeps direction and throws away length

cards.label: Residual stream
cards.title: A shared ledger nobody erases

1.plain: A shared bus every component reads from and writes to by addition, so the whole model is a sum of contributions.
1.pic: The residual stream is like a shared ledger: every worker reads the running totals, works something out and appends an entry, and nothing is ever rubbed out, so the final totals are the opening balance plus every entry and you can say exactly who contributed what.

2.what: The running vector that every attention head and MLP reads from and adds its output to, from the embedding to the unembedding.
2.when: Every time you build, read or edit a transformer: it is the object every interpretability tool points at.
2.why: Because every write is an addition, the model's output splits exactly into per-component contributions you can measure and change.

where: ResNet skip connections: the same additive idea in vision
Direct logit attribution and the logit lens, which read the sum term by term or layer by layer
Steering vectors, which add your own entry to the stream
Activation patching, which swaps one term of the sum for another

cards.label: Attention head
cards.title: Ask the class, copy the notes

1.plain: One head moves information from earlier positions to the current one, choosing where by a query–key match and what by a value–output map.
1.pic: An attention head is a pupil in a classroom of notebooks: it asks a question, every pupil sitting earlier holds up a label, the best matches fly their notes over by paper plane, and the pupil adds a summary of those notes into its own notebook.

2.what: The unit that moves information between positions: each position asks a question, matches it against earlier positions' labels and copies a blend of their contents.
2.when: In every layer of every transformer, and whenever you want to know which earlier tokens influenced the current one.
2.why: It is the only part of a transformer that moves information across positions (the MLPs work within one position), so circuits like induction heads live here.

where: Induction heads: a learned attention pattern that finds an earlier copy of the current token and reads what came next
KV caching: past keys and values never change, so they are stored and reused
Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio's translation model, where the decoder soft-searches every source word
Any soft lookup: match a query against keys, then take a weighted read of the values

cards.label: Softmax attention & the causal mask
cards.title: One whole pie, shared only backwards

1.plain: Scale the query–key scores by 1/sqrt(d_head), mask out future positions with negative infinity, then softmax over keys.
1.pic: Each token is a guest in a queue who cuts one whole pie into shares for the guests ahead of it, by how useful each looks, and the causal mask means guests behind are never invited to the cutting, rather than having their slices binned afterwards.

2.what: Scale query-key scores by 1/√d_head, set future positions to −∞, then softmax over keys so each position takes a normalised blend of earlier values.
2.when: In every head of every layer of a decoder-only transformer, on every forward pass.
2.why: It moves information between positions without letting a token see what it must predict, and masking before the softmax keeps every row a true distribution.

where: Illegal-move masking in game-playing policies: illegal logits go to −∞ before the softmax
Padding masks in batched attention, so real tokens ignore pad tokens
KV caching, which exists because under the mask past keys and values never change
Reading attention patterns in interpretability: an induction head is one learned pattern

cards.label: MLP layer
cards.title: Questions in, sticky notes out

1.plain: Two linear maps with a non-linearity between them, applied to each position independently.
1.pic: An MLP layer is a private desk each token visits alone: a wall of yes/no questions is checked against the token's notes, and every clear yes adds its matching sticky note back onto the notes.

2.what: Two linear maps with a nonlinearity between them, applied to every token position separately, with the output added back to the residual stream.
2.when: In every transformer block, right after attention has gathered information from other positions.
2.why: Attention only moves information around; the MLP is where each position does non-linear computation on what it gathered.

where: Sparse autoencoders and transcoders are themselves one-hidden-layer MLPs, built to be readable
The Q-networks and policy heads in the RL chapter are small MLPs
The classic 'neural network' in every textbook is exactly this: linear, squash, linear

cards.label: Transformer block
cards.title: A meeting, then quiet study

1.plain: Attention then MLP, each wrapped in LayerNorm and each writing back into the residual stream.
1.pic: A transformer block is like one shift for a row of words, each with its own notebook: first a meeting where each word may read earlier words' notebooks, then quiet study where each word thinks alone, and both shifts add notes without ever erasing.

2.what: The repeating unit of a transformer: attention, then an MLP, each reading a normalised copy of the residual stream and adding its output back.
2.when: Every time you build, load, train or take apart a transformer, which is most of this course.
2.why: Adding instead of overwriting keeps every earlier write readable and gives gradients a straight path back, so deep stacks train and can later be taken apart.

where: Every transformer, from GPT-2 to today's chat models and vision transformers, repeats this block
Interpretability: logit attribution, activation patching and steering all assume the additive stream
ResNets in vision: the same add-don't-overwrite skip path that lets deep stacks train

cards.label: Unembedding
cards.title: Every word scores the final arrow

1.plain: The final matrix turning a residual vector into logits over the vocabulary.
1.pic: The unembedding is a line of judges, one per word in the vocabulary, each holding their own arrow; they score the model's final arrow by how far it points along theirs, and those scores are the logits.

2.what: The final matrix that scores every vocabulary token by a dot product with the last residual vector, producing the logits.
2.when: At the end of every forward pass, and any time you want to read what an internal vector says in words.
2.why: Because it is linear, any piece of the residual stream can be read through it, which makes it the main window interpretability uses to see what a model is doing.

where: Logit lens: unembed the middle of the model to watch its guess form
Direct logit attribution: unembed each head's output to see what it pushes
OV circuits: W_U W_OV W_E, what a head writes about a token it attends to
Any classifier's final linear layer: one score per class, then softmax

cards.label: Training loop
cards.title: Shoot, score, blame, adjust, wipe

1.plain: Batch, forward, loss, backward, step, log — and a validation pass that tells you whether any of it worked.
1.pic: A training loop is an archer's practice routine: shoot a quiver, measure every miss, trace each miss to the part of the stance that caused it, adjust, wipe the board, write the score down, and now and then shoot at a separate target purely to check.

2.what: The repeated cycle of batch, forward, loss, backward, step and zero_grad, plus a validation pass that checks it worked.
2.when: Every time you train anything: a ResNet in [0.2], a transformer in [1.1], DQN and PPO in chapter 2.
2.why: Two of its steps are easy to omit and both fail quietly, so knowing the rhythm cold is how you spot a loop that runs but does not learn.

where: DQN and PPO in chapter 2: the same skeleton with a new loss and new data
Weights & Biases logging and sweeps, which wrap this loop
Distributed training, which shards this same loop across GPUs

cards.label: Sampling
cards.title: A raffle drum with three dials

1.plain: Turning a distribution over next tokens into an actual token — the step where all the decoding knobs live.
1.pic: Sampling is a raffle: every word holds tickets in proportion to its probability and you draw one, while temperature reprints the tickets, top-k keeps only the biggest holders in the drum, and top-p keeps the biggest holders until they cover a set share of all tickets.

2.what: The step that turns the model's next-token probabilities into one actual token, with temperature, top-k and top-p as the knobs.
2.when: Every time a language model writes text, one token at a time.
2.why: Likelihood is a good training objective but a bad decoding objective: always taking the top token gives bland, repetitive text, so how you draw shapes what the same model says.

where: The temperature, top_k and top_p parameters of every text-generation API
Beam search, which keeps several partial sentences instead of drawing one token at a time
Sampling actions from a softmax policy in RL, where temperature trades exploring against exploiting
Evals that sample the same prompt many times at T > 0 to measure how often a behaviour appears

cards.label: Temperature
cards.title: A contrast knob on the odds

1.plain: Divide the logits before the softmax: below 1 sharpens the distribution, above 1 flattens it.
1.pic: Temperature is like a contrast knob on the model's odds: low temperature is high contrast, so the likeliest word outshines the rest; high temperature is low contrast, so every word fades towards the same grey; and the order of brightness never changes.

2.what: A single number that divides the logits before the softmax, sharpening (T < 1) or flattening (T > 1) the next-token distribution.
2.when: Every time you sample from a model: low for reliable, repeatable answers, higher for variety.
2.why: It trades predictability against diversity without changing the model or the ranking of its guesses.

where: Scaled attention: dividing QKᵀ by √d_k acts as a fixed temperature that keeps the softmax from saturating
Knowledge distillation, where a higher temperature exposes more of a teacher's preferences
Softmax policies in RL, where a temperature trades exploring against exploiting
The Boltzmann distribution in physics, where the name comes from

cards.label: Hooks
cards.title: A worker at a named window

1.plain: Functions attached to a named activation that can read it, or return a modified version to replace it.
1.pic: A hook is like a worker you station at a named window beside a conveyor belt: every tray passing that window can be noted down or swapped for another, and the belt carries on with whatever the worker hands back.

2.what: A function attached to a named activation inside a running model, which can read it or hand back a replacement.
2.when: Whenever you ask a model 'what if': ablate a head, patch in another run, add a steering vector, or record a statistic mid-run.
2.why: Watching only shows correlation; changing an activation mid-run and seeing what happens downstream is how you get causal evidence.

where: Ablation, activation patching and path patching: a hook that zeroes or swaps an activation
Steering vectors and activation capping: a hook that adds to or clamps the residual stream
Outside ML: debugger watchpoints and web middleware, code that intercepts a value at a named point

cards.label: Attention pattern
cards.title: A chart of who looks at whom

1.plain: The (query, key) probability matrix for one head — the picture you look at first when asking what a head does.
1.pic: An attention pattern is the glance chart of a dinner party where guests arrive in order: each guest has exactly one unit of attention to split among the guests already seated, and the chart records who looked at whom and how much.

2.what: A head's matrix of attention weights, showing for each token how it splits its attention over earlier tokens.
2.when: The first thing you look at when asking what a head does, from [1.2] onwards in every circuit hunt.
2.why: It is the cheapest direct window into where information flows, which tells you which heads are worth testing properly.

where: Markov chains: a row-stochastic transition matrix, each row a split of probability
Cross-attention in translation and image-generation models: the same chart, with queries and keys from different sequences
Later circuits such as induction heads: first recognised by the shape of their pattern

cards.label: Ablation
cards.title: Mute one player, hear what breaks

1.plain: Delete a component — zero it, or replace it with its mean — and see how much performance you lose.
1.pic: Ablation is muting one player in an orchestra and listening to how much worse the piece gets; pure silence throws everyone off, so a fairer test has a stand-in play that player's usual part.

2.what: Removing one component's output, by zeroing it or replacing it with its mean, and measuring how much performance drops.
2.when: When you have a suspect component and want a first causal test of whether the model needs it.
2.why: Attention patterns only show correlation; knocking a part out shows necessity, as long as you watch for off-distribution shock and for backups covering.

where: Finding a minimal circuit: ablate everything outside it and check performance survives
Activation patching: the same surgery with a specific replacement instead of a blank
Ablation studies in ML papers: drop one design choice and compare
Gene knockouts in biology, with the same trap of redundant backups
3.judge: Current method: mean-ablation. Activation patching replaces with a specific alternative, a sharper causal question. Attribution patching approximates it with gradients, far cheaper.

cards.label: Induction head
cards.title: Find the stamp, copy the next word

1.plain: A head implementing 'I saw A then B earlier, I'm at A again, so predict B' — it attends to the token after the previous copy of the current token.
1.pic: An induction head is like a two-clerk filing trick: clerk one stamps every card with the word that came before it, and when a word shows up again, clerk two finds the card stamped with that word and copies whatever is written on it.

2.what: A pair of attention heads that implement 'I saw A then B earlier, I'm at A again, so predict B'.
2.when: Whenever a sequence repeats something from earlier in its context, from random tokens to names and code.
2.why: It is the first circuit where two heads cooperate, it explains a visible jump in in-context learning during training, and its stripe gives a cheap detector you can check causally.

where: In-context learning: Olsson et al. (2022) tied a jump in it during training to induction heads forming
Copying names, code identifiers and repeated phrases from earlier in a prompt
The guess, detect, ablate loop you reuse for IOI, path patching and bracket classifiers
K-composition generally: any later head that looks where an earlier head's writing tells it to

cards.label: Previous-token head
cards.title: Note down who came before

1.plain: A head that attends one position back, writing 'the token before me was X' into the residual stream.
1.pic: A previous-token head is like everyone in a queue glancing at the person just in front and sticking that name on a note on their own back, so a later searcher can ask 'who stood behind Alice?' and find the answer.

2.what: An attention head that looks one position back and writes the previous token's identity into the current position.
2.when: Early in the model, wherever later heads need to know 'what came just before me', most famously for induction.
2.why: Attention is the only way information moves between positions, and many later tricks depend on this one-step relay existing.

where: The first half of every induction circuit
The IOI circuit, where [1.4.1] validates previous-token heads by patching
Bigram-style prediction: knowing the previous word is the simplest basis for guessing the next
Shift registers and causal convolutions, which pass each value one step along

cards.label: Induction score
cards.title: Say it twice, see who points

1.plain: Average attention paid to the (offset by one) diagonal on a repeated random sequence — a number that ranks every head.
1.pic: The induction score is a déjà vu test: read fifty nonsense words aloud twice, and on the second pass measure how often each listener points at the word that followed the current word last time.

2.what: One number per attention head: its average attention along the induction stripe of a repeated random sequence.
2.when: When you need to find induction heads, or any head with a predictable pattern, across a whole model at once.
2.why: It turns eyeballing every attention pattern into a ranked heatmap, so careful causal checks can focus on a few candidates.

where: Finding name mover and S-inhibition heads in the IOI circuit with the same score-then-ablate loop
Previous-token and duplicate-token head detectors: the same diagonal trick at different offsets
Sweeping probes or SAE latents across layers: one number per component, then verify the bright ones

cards.label: Circuit
cards.title: The small team inside the office

1.plain: A small subgraph of heads and MLPs that, together, implements one identifiable behaviour.
1.pic: A circuit is like the small team inside a huge office that actually handles one job: everyone writes on one shared whiteboard, but only a few desks, passing notes that change where the next desk looks, get this particular answer out.

2.what: A small set of heads and MLPs, and the connections between them, that together carry out one identifiable behaviour.
2.when: When you want to explain how a model does a specific task, not just that it can.
2.why: It turns a capability into a mechanism with an address that you can test, and eventually edit or steer.

where: Induction heads: a two-head circuit (previous-token head plus induction head) in [1.2]
The balanced-bracket classifier in [1.5.1], where the true algorithm is known in advance
Feature-level circuits: attribution graphs over transcoder features in [1.4.2]
3.judge: Current method: circuits of heads and MLPs found with patching, as in IOI. Emerging: circuits of sparse features, since MLP neurons are polysemantic (transcoders, attribution graphs in [1.4.2]). You need: patching plus the three tests.

cards.label: QK circuit
cards.title: Who wants to listen to whom

1.plain: The composed matrix W_E W_Q W_K^T W_E^T that says which source tokens a head wants to attend to.
1.pic: A head's QK circuit is a preference chart printed before any party: for every pair of guests it says how keen the first is to turn and listen to the second, and on the night each guest reads their own row for the guests already there and shares out their attention.

2.what: A vocabulary-by-vocabulary table, made by multiplying a head's weights, saying how much each token wants to attend to each other token.
2.when: When you want to know where a head looks as a property of the model, before running any prompt.
2.why: Only the product W_Q W_Kᵀ affects attention, so reading it directly turns an opaque head into a table you can inspect.

where: The OV circuit: the same trick for what a head writes once it has looked
K-composition: a later head's keys built from an earlier head's output
Recommender systems scoring every user-item pair with a low-rank product of two thin tables

cards.label: OV circuit
cards.title: The head's phrasebook

1.plain: The composed matrix W_E W_V W_O W_U that says what a head writes to the logits once it attends somewhere.
1.pic: An OV circuit is like a head's phrasebook: once the head has decided which word to look at, it opens the phrasebook to that word's page and reads out which next words to vote for, and a copying head's phrasebook simply says each word back.

2.what: A head's value and output weights, sandwiched between embedding and unembedding and read as a table from 'token attended to' to 'logits pushed'.
2.when: Whenever you want to know what a head writes regardless of any particular prompt, for example to test whether it copies.
2.why: It turns four opaque matrices into one readable map, so claims like 'this head copies' can be checked straight from the weights.

where: Name-mover heads in IOI: OV circuits that copy a name into the logits
Induction heads: the copying half of the circuit that continues repeated text
The direct path W_E W_U, read the same way as a table of which token tends to follow which

cards.label: K-composition
cards.title: Find the tag that names you

1.plain: A later head's keys are built from an earlier head's output, so the two compose into one algorithm.
1.pic: K-composition is a two-host party trick: the first host writes on every guest's tag who stood just before them, and the second host finds 'whoever came after Alice' by searching those tags, not the guests themselves.

2.what: A later attention head builds its keys from what an earlier head wrote into the residual stream, so the two heads act as one algorithm.
2.when: Whenever a behaviour needs information that isn't at a position yet, like 'the token after the last copy of me' in induction.
2.why: A single head can only match what is already at each position; composition lets two layers express searches neither head could do alone.

where: Induction heads: the previous-token head writes, the induction head's keys read
IOI's circuit: later heads read what earlier heads wrote, through Q- and K-composition
Any system where one stage labels items so a later stage can search by label, like a database index
Composition scores: spotting which head pairs talk, from weights alone

cards.label: Q-composition
cards.title: Someone wrote on your shopping list

1.plain: A later head's queries are built from an earlier head's output.
1.pic: Q-composition is an earlier helper writing a line on a shopper's list: the stalls and their labels stay exactly the same, but what the shopper goes looking for has changed.

2.what: A later attention head building its query partly from an earlier head's output, so the earlier head changes what the later head looks for.
2.when: When tracing circuits such as IOI, where S-inhibition heads steer the name movers away from the repeated name.
2.why: It is one of only three ways heads can cooperate, and knowing which door a signal uses tells you how to test, ablate or steer it.

where: K-composition in induction heads: there the earlier head relabels the keys instead
Query rewriting in search and retrieval: an earlier step edits what the next lookup asks for
Circuit tracing in general: every head-to-head link is Q, K or V composition

cards.label: Logit lens
cards.title: A straw poll after every round

1.plain: Apply the unembedding to an intermediate residual vector and read what the model would have said if it stopped there.
1.pic: The logit lens is like calling a straw poll after every round of a jury's deliberation: using the official counting rules, you ask 'if you had to vote right now, what would you say?', and watch when the verdict forms.

2.what: Running an intermediate residual state through the model's own final LayerNorm and unembedding, to read what it would predict if it stopped there.
2.when: When you want a cheap first look at where in the stack a prediction forms, before any patching.
2.why: It needs no training or intervention, it shows the stream is a running prediction, and where it disagrees with the model, the gap points at what later layers do.

where: Direct logit attribution: the same projection split per component instead of per layer
An SAE or transcoder latent's logit lens: its decoder vector dotted with W_U
Checking what a steering vector will push the model to say, with no forward pass
The tuned lens, which swaps the borrowed decoder for a trained one per layer
3.judge: Current method: the raw lens, which works well on GPT-2. Research (Belrose et al.) finds it brittle on other families and trains a tuned lens. What you need: the raw lens on GPT-2, tested on a known case.

cards.label: Direct logit attribution
cards.title: Score every pull on the rope

1.plain: Project each component's write onto the logit-difference direction to get its signed contribution to the answer.
1.pic: Direct logit attribution is like scoring a tug of war pull by pull: the rope runs from 'John' to 'Mary', every head pulls with its own arrow, and only the part of each pull along the rope counts, so the pulls add up exactly to the final result.

2.what: Splitting the model's answer, a logit difference, into one signed number per component by projecting each component's output onto the answer direction.
2.when: As the cheap first pass whenever you want to know which heads or layers produce a behaviour, before any patching.
2.why: The residual stream is a sum and the logit difference is linear, so the split is exact and costs a single cached forward pass.

where: The logit lens: the same projection applied to the whole stream at one layer
Direct feature attribution: the same trick with SAE features instead of heads
Linear probes: any linear readout of a sum splits across the sum's terms
Algorithmic-task interpretability, where DLA shortlists components in toy models
