cards.label: Linear probe
cards.title: One straight line across the crowd

1.plain: Train a small linear classifier on frozen activations to test whether a property is linearly readable there.
1.pic: A linear probe is like a referee allowed one straight chalk line across a crowded hall: if the line cleanly splits guests wearing 'true' badges from 'false' ones, the model keeps truth somewhere readable at that moment, and whether the model actually uses that line is a separate test where you…

2.what: A tiny linear classifier trained on a frozen model's activations to test whether a property is linearly readable at that layer.
2.when: When you have one specific question about what a model represents (truth, deception, a board state) and labelled examples to ask it with.
2.why: It's the cheapest window into a model, one direction and a dot product, but it only shows what is readable; patching shows what the model uses.

where: Deception probes: the same tool aimed at intent instead of fact (Apollo Research, 2025)
OthelloGPT: probing a game-playing model for a board it was never shown
Steering vectors: the same kind of direction, added in to change behaviour rather than read out
Activation oracles: swapping the probe's one fixed yes/no question for open-ended ones

cards.label: Probe-directed intervention
cards.title: Warm the dial, watch the heating

1.plain: Push activations along a probe's direction and check the behaviour moves — the causal test a correlational probe can't give you.
1.pic: Probe-directed intervention is like finding a dial on the wall that tracks the room's temperature, then warming it with your hand: if the heating clicks off, the building really reads that dial; if nothing happens, it was only a thermometer on the wall.

2.what: Adding a scaled probe direction to a model's activations with a hook, then checking whether the model's behaviour shifts: the causal test a correlational probe cannot give you.
2.when: Right after a probe works: before you claim the model uses a property, and before you build any steering on that direction.
2.why: Probes fit whatever separates the labels, confounds included; only moving the model's own output shows the direction is used, and in Marks and Tegmark the most accurate probe was not the most causal.

where: Steering vectors, its sibling: the same push, usually along a difference of means over contrasting prompts
Activation patching: another causal test, swapping in activations from a different input instead of adding a direction
Deception probes: the same probing question asked about intent rather than fact
Science in general: a correlation earns the word 'cause' only when you intervene and the outcome moves

cards.label: Indirect object identification (IOI)
cards.title: Skip the name you've heard twice

1.plain: The behaviour where 'John and Mary went to the shops, John gave a bag to' is completed with ' Mary' — a task small enough to reverse-engineer completely.
1.pic: IOI is like a mail room where early clerks stamp the second 'John' as a repeat, couriers carry a 'John is taken' note to the front desk, and the front-desk clerks copy onto the reply whichever name is not on the note: Mary.

2.what: A one-template task, two names with one repeated, that GPT-2 small completes with the other name, reverse-engineered as 26 of its 144 heads in seven classes.
2.when: Whenever you need the reference example of finding, and proving, a circuit in a real pretrained model.
2.why: It set explicit standards (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) for when a mechanism story counts as found rather than merely fitting the plots.

where: Automated circuit discovery: the same find-and-verify process, run by a script
Attribution graphs, which trace a behaviour through learned features instead of whole heads
Designing corrupted prompts for activation and path patching in any interpretability study
Every week-8 tool: direct logit attribution, activation patching and path patching are all demonstrated on IOI

cards.label: Logit difference
cards.title: A balance, not a gauge

1.plain: Use logit(correct) minus logit(distractor) as the metric, because it cancels everything the two share.
1.pic: Logit difference is like weighing the right answer against the wrong one on a balance: whatever lands equally in both pans cancels, every helper's weights simply add to the tilt, and unlike a percentage gauge the beam never pins at the top.

2.what: The model's score for the right answer minus its score for the tempting wrong one: the log of how many times likelier one is than the other.
2.when: Whenever you intervene inside a model (attribution, patching, steering) and need to measure the effect on one specific choice.
2.why: It cancels everything the two answers share, never saturates, and is linear in the residual stream, so effects add up and can be split per component.

where: Reward models in RLHF score preferences as sigmoid(r_A − r_B): a difference of scores
Log-odds in statistics and logistic regression: a probability ratio on a log scale
Steering and probing metrics: measure a behaviour as 'desired token minus undesired token'

cards.label: Activation patching
cards.title: Swap one baton from the good race

1.plain: Run on a corrupted prompt, splice one activation in from the clean run, and measure how much of the correct behaviour returns.
1.pic: Activation patching is running two identical relay races, one with the right message and one with a single word changed, then handing one runner in the broken race the baton from the same lane and leg of the good race, and seeing whether the right answer reaches the finish.

2.what: A causal test: run on a corrupted prompt, overwrite one activation with its clean-run value, and measure how much of the right behaviour returns.
2.when: As the first move in a circuit investigation, once you have a matched clean and corrupted prompt pair and a signed metric.
2.why: Reading activations shows correlation; swapping them one at a time shows which ones actually carry the behaviour.

where: Debugging by swapping one part from a working machine into a broken one
Knockout and rescue experiments in biology: necessity and sufficiency again
Path patching and attribution patching, its narrower and faster cousins
Locating a stored fact in a language model, then editing it (ROME)

cards.label: Denoising vs noising
cards.title: Which kitchen gets the swap?

1.plain: Denoising patches clean activations into a corrupted run and asks what is sufficient; noising does the reverse and asks what is necessary.
1.pic: Denoising versus noising is like swapping one cook between a good kitchen and a sabotaged one: send a good cook into the sabotaged kitchen and see if the dish is rescued (enough), or a sabotaged cook into the good kitchen and see if the dish is ruined (needed).

2.what: The two directions of activation patching: clean values into a corrupted run (denoising) or corrupted values into a clean run (noising).
2.when: Every time you run a patching experiment and write down what it showed.
2.why: Denoising tests sufficiency and noising tests necessity, and redundant or jointly-acting parts answer the two differently, so the direction decides the claim.

where: Path patching and circuit discovery, where the direction decides which edges you keep
Ablation studies anywhere in ML: removing a part tests necessity, adding it alone tests sufficiency
Reliability engineering: redundant backups hide from single-failure tests, two-key systems fail any single removal

cards.label: Path patching
cards.title: Tap one wire, freeze the rest

1.plain: Patch an activation but let only one downstream route see the change, so you measure an edge rather than a node.
1.pic: Path patching is testing one hallway in an office: send a doctored memo from Alice straight to Bob, order everyone else to repeat exactly what they said on the good day, and see whether Bob's decision changes.

2.what: Changing only what one component sends directly to another, with every other attention head frozen at its clean value, to measure an edge instead of a node.
2.when: Once you already suspect who talks to whom, after activation patching has told you which components matter.
2.why: A list of important parts is not a mechanism; edges are, and only an edge-level intervention can tell 'A matters via B' from 'A matters some other way'.

where: IOI: turning a list of important heads into a circuit graph
Automated circuit discovery: this edge-by-edge sweep run as a search
Telling Q-, K- and V-composition apart by patching queries, keys or values
Outside ML: mediation analysis, splitting a cause's direct effect from its effect through a middleman

cards.label: Name-mover head
cards.title: The announcer reads the other name

1.plain: A late head that attends to the non-duplicated name and copies it into the logits.
1.pic: A name mover is a stadium announcer at the final microphone: told not to read the name that came up twice, he looks over at the other name card and reads it out, and the harder he looks at a card, the louder that name comes out.

2.what: A late attention head that attends from the final token to the name that was not repeated and copies it into the output logits.
2.when: When you study the IOI circuit in week 4, and whenever you look for the heads that directly write a model's answer.
2.why: It is where the circuit's reasoning becomes output, so it is the natural place to start tracing, and the classic lesson in why ablation can hide a role.

where: Induction heads: the same look-then-copy move, keyed on what came next last time
Copy mechanisms in summarisation models: attend to a source word, then copy it out
Any circuit hunt: find the heads that write the answer first, then trace back

cards.label: Backup name-mover head
cards.title: The understudy steps in

1.plain: A head that takes over the name-moving job when the primary name movers are ablated.
1.pic: A backup name-mover head is like an understudy: while the lead delivers the key line it waits in the wings, but when the lead is knocked out it steps on and says the same line, so the show barely changes and a careless critic concludes the lead never mattered.

2.what: Heads that take over the name-moving job in GPT-2 small's IOI circuit when the primary name movers are ablated.
2.when: Whenever you test a component's importance by removing it and the score barely moves.
2.why: Self-repair means a single ablation number is not evidence of unimportance, so claims about what a model needs, or can no longer do, must account for backups.

where: Any interpretability ablation study: report direct effects next to the drop
Safety claims like 'we removed the circuit, so the capability is gone', which backups can quietly falsify
Networks trained with dropout, which are pushed to spread one job across redundant units
Engineering with hot spares, where failover hides the primary's importance until both fail

cards.label: Minimality & faithfulness
cards.title: Can the skeleton crew sail?

1.plain: Tests that the circuit you propose is both enough to do the task and has no spare parts.
1.pic: Checking a circuit is like vetting a skeleton crew for a ship: it must sail as well as the full company when everyone else is replaced by stand-ins who only do the average job (faithful), sending the same people home from both must hurt both equally (complete), and every crew member must be needed…

2.what: Three tests of a proposed circuit: it does the task alone (faithful), nothing important lies outside it (complete), and every part matters somewhere (minimal).
2.when: After patching gives you a candidate circuit, and before you believe it or build interventions on it.
2.why: Diagrams that fit the plots can still be wrong; these tests turn a story into a checkable claim, even when backup heads hide importance.

where: Any circuit you find later, whether built from heads, SAE features or transcoder latents
Minimal bug reproductions: enough to trigger the bug, nothing extra
Ablation studies in ML papers: remove a part and check whether the result survives
Engineering redundancy: a backup hides how much the primary matters until both fail

cards.label: Feature
cards.title: A compass bearing you can name

1.plain: A direction in activation space that corresponds to something a human can name.
1.pic: A feature is a compass bearing on the model's map of activations: each activation is a spot on the map, how much of the feature it holds is how far it lies along that bearing, and the bearings rarely follow the map's printed grid lines, which are the neurons.

2.what: A direction in a model's activation space that corresponds to something a human can name.
2.when: Whenever you try to read, find or change what a model represents, from probes to sparse autoencoders to steering.
2.why: Neurons are often polysemantic and there can be more features than dimensions, so directions, not neurons, are the unit that carries meaning.

where: Linear probes: a learned direction that reads one feature out of the residual stream
Steering vectors: add a feature direction to push the model's behaviour
Sparse autoencoders: learn an overcomplete dictionary of feature directions
3.judge: Current method: assume the linear representation hypothesis and hunt for directions. Open question: how far it holds. What you need: confirm a named feature by intervening along it, not only by reading examples.

cards.label: Linear representation hypothesis
cards.title: Concepts are directions you can walk

1.plain: Models represent concepts as directions, so a concept can be read out by a projection and edited by an addition.
1.pic: A model's state is like your position in a city where every idea is a street running in its own direction: how far along a street you stand reads that idea, and walking along it changes that idea while leaving the cross streets alone.

2.what: The hypothesis that models store concepts as directions in activation space, readable by a projection and editable by an addition.
2.when: Whenever you probe, steer or decompose activations: the whole interpretability toolkit leans on it.
2.why: Where it holds, simple linear tools can read and control a model's concepts; where it fails they mislead, so every finding gets a causal test.

where: Linear probes: reading one concept with one dot product
Steering vectors: changing behaviour by adding one direction
Sparse autoencoders: finding thousands of such directions at once
Word-vector arithmetic, the classic early sign that meaning can live in directions
3.judge: Current practice treats concepts as directions: probes, steering vectors and SAEs all assume it. Open question: not every feature need be a simple direction. What you need: default to linear, verify causally.

cards.label: Superposition
cards.title: Five lodgers, two rooms

1.plain: A layer represents more features than it has dimensions by storing them as non-orthogonal directions and paying interference as the cost.
1.pic: Superposition is like fitting five lodgers into a two-room flat: it works because they are rarely home at the same time, and the price is the occasional collision in the hallway.

2.what: A layer storing more features than it has dimensions by giving them overlapping, non-orthogonal directions and tolerating the interference.
2.when: When features are sparse, each rarely active, which is what switches it on in the toy models; it is the leading explanation for polysemantic neurons.
2.why: It is why single neurons are a poor unit of analysis and why sparse autoencoders are needed to recover readable features.

where: Polysemantic neurons in real language models, the symptom superposition is proposed to explain
Sparse autoencoders, built to pull the overlapping features back apart into readable directions
Deep double descent, whose two phases Anthropic tie to datapoints versus features held in superposition
Compressed sensing: recovering a sparse signal from fewer measurements than unknowns

cards.label: Polysemanticity
cards.title: One microphone, several singers

1.plain: One neuron fires for several unrelated things, so reading neurons one at a time doesn't work.
1.pic: A polysemantic neuron is one microphone in a choir recorded with fewer microphones than singers: every mic picks up a blend of voices, so listening to one mic you hear unrelated singers at once.

2.what: One neuron firing for several unrelated things, so a single neuron is not a single concept.
2.when: Whenever you read a model neuron by neuron, especially in layers that must hold many more concepts than they have neurons.
2.why: It is why interpretability works with directions and dictionary features instead of individual neurons.

where: Sparse autoencoders and transcoders, built to un-mix polysemantic activations
The cocktail party problem: separating many voices from a few microphones
Compressed sensing: recovering a sparse signal from fewer measurements than unknowns
3.judge: Polysemanticity is the symptom. Superposition is one proposed cause, not a synonym. A neuron can be polysemantic because features just don't line up with neurons, or because the layer stores more features than it has neurons. Only the second is superposition.

cards.label: Feature sparsity
cards.title: Sell more tickets than seats

1.plain: Most features are absent from most inputs, which is exactly the condition that makes superposition worth it to the model.
1.pic: Feature sparsity is like an airline overbooking a flight: because most ticket-holders rarely show up, two of them almost never turn up for the same seat, so selling more tickets than seats is a good bet.

2.what: The fact that most features are absent from most inputs, so any two of them are rarely active at the same time.
2.when: Whenever you ask why a model overlaps features instead of dropping them, or why an SAE's sparsity penalty can pull them apart.
2.why: Interference only costs when overlapping features co-occur, and co-occurrence shrinks like p², far faster than the benefit p of representing each feature.

where: Superposition: the geometry a model builds when its features are sparse
Sparse autoencoders: dictionary learning that relies on features being rarely active
Compressed sensing and hash tables: fitting sparse things into fewer slots than there are things

cards.label: Interference
cards.title: The mic hears the neighbours

1.plain: Because superposed features aren't orthogonal, activating one leaks a little into the others.
1.pic: Interference is five singers crowded onto a small stage with one directional mic: aim it at one singer and you still hear the neighbours, in proportion to how close they stand, unless they are silent or a noise gate mutes them.

2.what: The leak between features stored as overlapping directions: reading one picks up a bit of every feature it overlaps with.
2.when: Whenever a network stores more features than it has dimensions, which superposition says is normal when features are sparse.
2.why: It is the price of superposition, and its shape (free when negative, cheap when sparse) explains the geometry models choose and the side effects of steering.

where: Polysemantic neurons: one neuron responding to several unrelated things
Sparse autoencoders: learning many directions to pull superposed features apart
Steering side effects: pushing one direction also nudges features that overlap it
Crosstalk and compressed sensing: sparse signals sharing too few channels

cards.label: Sparse autoencoder (SAE)
cards.title: A short recipe from a huge pantry

1.plain: A wide, sparsely-activating autoencoder trained to reconstruct an activation as a sum of a few dictionary directions.
1.pic: A sparse autoencoder is a taster who rewrites a smoothie as a recipe card: a few ingredients, with amounts, picked from a pantry far bigger than the list of tastes, and the card must remake the same smoothie.

2.what: A wide autoencoder that rewrites one layer's activation as a few active directions from a much larger learned dictionary.
2.when: When neurons are too tangled to read, which in language models is almost always, because superposition packs in more features than neurons.
2.why: It turns a jumble of polysemantic neurons into thousands of mostly readable latents you can inspect, ablate and steer.

where: Gemma Scope: open SAE suites you load with SAELens in [1.3.3]
Transcoders: the same idea applied to a layer's input-to-output map
Steering with a latent: clamp it and see whether behaviour follows
Classic sparse coding: a signal written as a few atoms from an overcomplete dictionary
3.judge: Current practice: load pretrained SAEs (Gemma Scope) with SAELens and read Neuronpedia dashboards. Emerging: absorption and splitting mean sparser is not reliably more interpretable.

cards.label: SAE latent
cards.title: A sniff test and a spoon

1.plain: One dictionary entry: an encoder direction that detects it and a decoder direction that writes it back.
1.pic: An SAE latent is one jar in a huge spice rack: its sniff test says how much of that spice is in the dish, its spoon adds exactly that flavour back, and any one dish uses only a few jars.

2.what: One entry in a sparse autoencoder's dictionary: an encoder direction that detects a pattern in a layer's activations and a decoder direction that writes it back.
2.when: When you want readable, steerable units instead of polysemantic neurons, at one chosen hook point.
2.why: Latents turn a tangle of neurons into handles you can inspect, attribute to and steer with, as long as you treat each name as a hypothesis to test.

where: Steering by adding a latent's decoder direction to the residual stream
Direct feature attribution and attribution patching, which credit a behaviour to individual latents
Transcoders, whose latents stand in for an MLP's input-to-output map
Autointerp, where an LLM writes and scores an explanation for each latent

cards.label: L1 sparsity penalty
cards.title: A flat fee to speak up

1.plain: The term that pushes most latents to zero — the single dial that trades reconstruction against interpretability.
1.pic: The L1 penalty is like a flat fee for speaking at a committee: every unit of talk costs the same, so members with only a small point say exactly nothing, and the size of the fee decides whether the committee is silent, chatty or usefully brief.

2.what: The term λ·Σ|fᵢ| in an SAE's loss that charges for every unit of latent activation, pushing most latents to exactly zero.
2.when: Whenever you train a sparse autoencoder, or judge one by its L0, dead and dense counts.
2.why: It is the single dial between faithful reconstruction and a short, readable list of active latents.

where: Lasso regression: the same flat penalty picks out a few features in statistics
Transcoders, which learn an MLP's input-to-output map under the same sparsity pressure
Compressed sensing: recovering a sparse signal from few measurements
Weight pruning, where a flat penalty drives whole weights to zero
3.judge: Current method in ARENA: ReLU + L1. Newer SAEs swap it for JumpReLU (GemmaScope) or TopK. What you need: the trade-off, and how to read L0, dead and dense latents.

cards.label: Max activating examples
cards.title: The dog's ten loudest barks

1.plain: Run a corpus, keep the inputs where a latent fires hardest, and read them to guess what it means.
1.pic: Reading max activating examples is like working out what a dog barks at from its ten loudest barks of the year: vivid and useful, but it describes the dog's most extreme moments, not most of its barking.

2.what: The corpus inputs where a latent fires hardest, read to form a first guess at what it means.
2.when: As the first look at any new neuron or SAE latent, always alongside its activation density, logit effects and a scored prediction.
2.why: They are the fastest way to a hypothesis and the fastest way to fool yourself, because they only show the extreme tail.

where: Autointerp: a language model writing, then scoring, explanations built from these examples
Feature dashboards on Neuronpedia: top examples beside density, logit effects and explanations
Survivorship bias: judging a strategy by its most famous winners

cards.label: Autointerp
cards.title: Write the guide, then go spotting

1.plain: Have a language model write an explanation of a latent from its top examples, then score the explanation by whether it predicts activations on held-out text.
1.pic: Autointerp is like writing a field-guide entry for a mystery bird from its best photos, then handing only the entry to a birdwatcher with a fresh album: the entry counts only if they tick the right photos.

2.what: Using one language model to explain a latent from its top examples, and another to test that explanation by predicting activations on new text.
2.when: Whenever you label SAE latents or neurons at scale, or read a label on a dashboard such as Neuronpedia.
2.why: A label that reads well can still be wrong; only its predictions on held-out text show whether it captures what the latent actually does.

where: Model-graded scoring in evals: one model judging another, which needs its own checks
Activation oracles: pointing a language model at another model's internals to get English back
Science in general: a hypothesis earns trust by predicting held-out data, not by reading well
3.judge: Current practice: the sparsity/reconstruction Pareto frontier. Emerging: autointerp scoring as a separate axis. What you need: treat every label as a scored hypothesis, never a fact.

cards.label: Attribution patching
cards.title: Read the slope, skip the experiment
cards.objectTitle: The hillside and its flat map

1.plain: A gradient-based linear approximation to patching, cheap enough to run over every latent at once.
1.pic: Attribution patching is estimating what each of thousands of dimmer switches does to a lamp by measuring how touchy each switch is and multiplying by how far you would turn it, instead of turning every switch off and re-measuring the room.

2.what: A shortcut that estimates what patching or ablating each component would do, as gradient times activation change, for every component at once.
2.when: When there are too many components to patch one by one, like the 16k latents of an SAE in [1.3.3].
2.why: It turns thousands of experiments into one backward pass, but it is a straight-line guess, so the important or surprising hits get confirmed with real patching.

where: Saliency maps: gradient × input as a quick guess at which pixels matter
Attribution graphs: the same gradient trick, made well defined by freezing attention patterns and LayerNorm scales
Sensitivity analysis in engineering: estimate each input's effect from derivatives instead of rerunning the simulation

cards.label: SAE steering
cards.title: Add a scoop, taste the change

1.plain: Clamp or add a specific latent during generation to test whether it causes the behaviour you think it means.
1.pic: SAE steering is testing a labelled ingredient by adding an extra scoop while blending and tasting the result: if the label says banana, the smoothie should now taste of banana, and if it tastes of something else, the label was wrong.

2.what: Turning one SAE latent up, by adding its direction or clamping its value, during generation to see whether the model does what the latent's label claims.
2.when: Whenever you need to know if a latent causes a behaviour rather than merely co-occurring with it, or want a precise, reversible handle on output.
2.why: Labels come from correlation; only an intervention shows cause, and the same intervention doubles as a practical steering tool.

where: The Golden Gate Bridge demo: one clamped feature changing Claude's self-description
Steering vectors from contrast pairs, like Love minus Hate in GPT-2-XL
Activation capping: a clamp that only acts when a direction exceeds a ceiling
Ablating a latent: the same hook with the scoop set to zero

library.label: JumpReLU SAE
library.title: Clear the bar or stay out
library.plain: Use a learned per-latent threshold with a straight-through gradient estimator instead of a plain ReLU.

cards.label: Markov decision process
cards.title: Squares, moves, dice and coins

1.plain: States, actions, a transition rule and a reward — the whole formal object RL optimises inside.
1.pic: A Markov decision process is a board game: squares, the moves allowed on each, dice that decide where you land using only your square and your move, coins you pick up, and coins that lose a little value for every turn you wait.

2.what: The formal game RL optimises inside: states, actions, transitions that depend only on the current state and action, rewards, and a discount.
2.when: Before writing any RL code: define the MDP, and solve a tiny one by hand so you know what right looks like.
2.why: Every algorithm from Q-learning to PPO and RLHF is defined relative to it, and many failures trace back to a mis-specified state, reward or discount.

where: Multi-armed bandits: the MDP with a single state
SARSA, Q-learning and DQN: solving an MDP when the rules are hidden and must be sampled
RLHF: text generation as an MDP, with tokens as actions and a reward model's score at the end
Planning by search, as in MCTS, inside a known MDP

cards.label: Policy
cards.title: A signpost at every crossroads

1.plain: A rule mapping states to actions, or to a distribution over actions.
1.pic: A policy is like a signpost at every crossroads: a plain sign points one way (deterministic), a spinner sign shows the odds for each road (stochastic), and following the signs from any start gives a route.

2.what: The agent's decision rule: a map from each state to an action, or to a probability for each action.
2.when: In every RL problem; it is what all RL algorithms, from Q-learning to PPO and RLHF, are trying to improve.
2.why: Values score situations, but only the policy acts, so it is where behaviour actually lives.

where: Language models: context is the state, the next token is the action, the softmax is the policy
Game-playing agents such as AlphaZero, whose network outputs a policy over moves
Thermostats and controllers: a fixed rule from reading to action
Policy iteration in [2.1], which rewrites a tabular policy until it stops changing

cards.label: Discount factor
cards.title: Fog over the road ahead

1.plain: Gamma: how much a reward one step later is worth, which also keeps infinite-horizon returns finite.
1.pic: The discount factor is fog over the road ahead: a coin one step away looks γ times its size, two steps away γ² times, so distant coins fade from view, you effectively see about 1/(1 − γ) steps, and the fog is what keeps an endless road's total view finite.

2.what: A number γ between 0 and 1 saying how much a reward one step later is worth compared with the same reward now.
2.when: In every return, value function and TD update an RL agent computes, except fixed-length set-ups like ARENA's RLHF, which drop it.
2.why: It keeps infinite sums finite and evaluation convergent, and it sets how far ahead the agent effectively plans.

where: Reward-to-go in REINFORCE: G_t = Σ γ^(i−t) r_i
GAE, where γ and λ compound into an effective horizon of about 1/(1 − γλ)
Exact policy evaluation, v = (I − γP)⁻¹r, which exists only when γ < 1
Exponential moving averages and present value in finance: the same geometric fade

cards.label: Value function
cards.title: Every square wears a points forecast

1.plain: The expected discounted return from a state, following a given policy.
1.pic: A value function is like a sticky note on every square of a board game saying how many points you will collect from there on, on average, if you keep playing your usual way, with points later counting a little less.

2.what: A number for every state: the expected discounted reward from there onwards if you keep following a given policy.
2.when: Whenever an agent must judge situations rather than single moves: planning, actor-critic, PPO and RLHF all keep one.
2.why: It compresses a long, uncertain future into one number per state, which lets credit flow backwards and lets you compare plans.

where: The critic in actor-critic and the value head in PPO
RLHF's value head on a language model
Pricing anything that pays out over time: future payments discounted back to today
Q-values, the state-action version that lets an agent choose greedily

cards.label: Q-value
cards.title: A price tag on every door

1.plain: The expected return from taking one specific action in a state and following the policy afterwards.
1.pic: A Q-value is like a price tag on every door out of a room, telling you how much treasure you will collect on average if you go through that door now and then carry on with your usual habits.

2.what: The expected total reward from taking one specific action in a state and then following your policy.
2.when: Whenever an agent must choose between actions without a model of the world, from tabular Q-learning to DQN.
2.why: Scoring each action directly turns choosing into 'take the biggest', and its gap from V (the advantage) is the signal that drives policy training.

where: DQN: a neural network that outputs one Q-value per action, the Q-table generalised
Advantage, A = Q − V, which weights the updates in actor-critic methods, PPO and RLHF
Tree search: MCTS keeps a running value estimate for each move from each node

cards.label: Bellman equation
cards.title: Coins now, plus where you land

1.plain: A value equals the immediate reward plus the discounted value of where you land — the recursion everything else is a way of solving.
1.pic: On a board game with a fixed plan, a square is worth the coins you grab leaving it plus a slightly shrunk share of what the square you land on is worth, so every square's worth is written in terms of its neighbours' and the numbers settle by passing guesses back and forth.

2.what: The rule that a state's value is its immediate reward plus the discounted value of where you land, averaged over where you might land.
2.when: Whenever you need to score states or actions over long futures: planning, value learning, every critic in RL.
2.why: It swaps an impossible infinite sum for a one-step recursion you can iterate or solve exactly, and every RL value method is a way of solving it.

where: TD learning: nudge V(s) towards r + γV(s′) from sampled steps
Q-learning and DQN: the same recursion with a max over next actions
Shortest paths (Bellman-Ford): each node's distance is one step plus its best neighbour's
Finance: a bond is worth this year's coupon plus next year's discounted price

cards.label: Policy evaluation
cards.title: Rewrite the notes until they settle

1.plain: Compute the value of a fixed policy by iterating the Bellman equation to a fixed point.
1.pic: Policy evaluation is like a board game where every square keeps a sticky note saying 'what I will collect from here if I follow the plan': each round every note is rewritten from the notes one step ahead, so news of each prize spreads outward a square per round, shrinking a little each step, until…

2.what: Working out how much reward a fixed plan collects from each state, by applying the Bellman equation repeatedly until the numbers stop changing.
2.when: Before improving a policy, and inside every RL method that learns a value function or a critic.
2.why: You cannot improve a plan you cannot score, and the Bellman rewrite turns 'sum over all futures' into a local rule that provably settles.

where: Q-learning and DQN: the same Bellman backup, with samples instead of the full map
The critic in actor-critic and PPO: a network trained to do policy evaluation
PageRank and heat diffusion: values that settle by repeatedly averaging their neighbours

cards.label: Policy improvement
cards.title: Pick the best turn at every junction

1.plain: Given values, take the greedy action in every state — the new policy is never worse.
1.pic: Policy improvement is rerouting with a scored map: at every junction, add the reward on each road to the old plan's score for where that road lands, and take the best one; a plan built this way is never worse anywhere.

2.what: Build a new plan by taking, in every state, the action with the best one-step lookahead under the current plan's values.
2.when: Right after evaluating a policy, as the second half of policy iteration, and implicitly whenever an agent acts greedily on its value estimates.
2.why: It is guaranteed never to make things worse, so alternating it with evaluation climbs to an optimal policy in a finite number of rounds.

where: Policy iteration: alternate exact evaluation with this greedy step until nothing changes
Q-learning and DQN: act greedily on estimated Q-values
Sat-nav rerouting: pick the turn that minimises cost now plus estimated time from there
RLHF: improving a policy against a learned reward, and why it needs a leash

cards.label: Policy iteration
cards.title: Repaint the signposts until none change

1.plain: Alternate evaluation and improvement until the policy stops changing.
1.pic: Policy iteration is improving a park's signposts: walk the park following the current signs and write down what each square is worth, then repaint every sign toward its best-looking neighbour, and repeat until no sign wants repainting.

2.what: Alternating two steps, scoring the current plan in every state and then switching each state to its best-looking action, until the plan stops changing.
2.when: Whenever you know the full rules of a small world (transition and reward tables), as in the [2.1] gridworld exercises.
2.why: Each round can only help and there are finitely many plans, so it must stop, and it stops at an optimal one; later RL methods are this loop with the map removed.

where: SARSA and Q-learning: the same loop, with sampled experience instead of a known map
Actor-critic methods, including the PPO used in RLHF: a critic evaluates, the actor improves
k-means clustering: assign, re-centre, repeat until nothing changes

cards.label: TD error
cards.title: Update the guess at every landmark

1.plain: The gap between your current value estimate and reward-plus-next-estimate — the learning signal for every bootstrapping method.
1.pic: TD error is the surprise on a drive home: at each landmark you add the minutes the last leg took to your fresh guess of the minutes left, compare that with your old guess, and correct the old guess straight away instead of waiting until you are home.

2.what: The gap between what you predicted from here and what you predict after one real step: r + γV(s') − V(s).
2.when: In every update of every bootstrapping RL method: SARSA, Q-learning, DQN, the critic in actor-critic and PPO, and GAE.
2.why: It lets an agent learn after each step instead of waiting for the end, trading a little bias for far less noise.

where: Q-learning and SARSA: tables updated by δ
DQN: a network trained to drive the squared TD error to zero
The critic in actor-critic and PPO, and GAE's sum of discounted δs
Any forecaster that corrects today's forecast from tomorrow's

cards.label: Epsilon-greedy
cards.title: Mostly the favourite, sometimes a gamble

1.plain: Take the greedy action most of the time and a random one with probability epsilon, so you keep exploring.
1.pic: Epsilon-greedy is like eating at your favourite restaurant most nights but rolling a ten-sided die first: on a 1 you try somewhere at random, so a better place can still turn up.

2.what: A behaviour policy that takes the best-looking action most of the time and a uniformly random one with probability ε.
2.when: In value-based RL (SARSA, Q-learning, DQN), whenever the agent must keep trying actions its current estimates undervalue.
2.why: Without exploration, early mistakes in the value estimates are never corrected; ε-greedy is the simplest way to keep every action in play.

where: DQN's replay buffer, filled with ε-greedy experience while ε decays on a linear schedule
Multi-armed bandits, where UCB and Thompson sampling are smarter alternatives
A/B tests and recommender systems that reserve a slice of traffic for trying new options
RL fine-tuning of language models, where sampling decides which behaviours ever get rewarded

cards.label: Q-learning
cards.title: Score as if you'll walk perfectly

1.plain: Update towards the reward plus the best next Q-value, regardless of what you actually did next.
1.pic: Q-learning is like writing a trail guidebook that scores each step as 'the reward just earned plus the best score listed at the next spot', as if you will walk perfectly from then on, even while you are still stumbling about.

2.what: A way to learn how good each move is by nudging its score towards the reward plus the best score available at the next state.
2.when: When you cannot see the environment's rules and must learn from experience, especially old or someone else's experience.
2.why: The max makes the target independent of how the data was collected, which enables replay buffers and DQN, at the price of optimistic values.

where: DQN: the same update with a neural network in place of the table
Replay buffers and learning from logged data, made legal by off-policy updates
Double DQN, which carries the fix for maximisation bias to neural networks
The winner's curse: picking the best of many noisy bids tends to overpay

cards.label: DQN
cards.title: Shuffled diary, frozen answer key

1.plain: Q-learning where the Q-table is replaced by a neural network, stabilised by a replay buffer and a target network.
1.pic: DQN is like a student who swaps a giant table of move scores for a trained gut feeling, studies from a shuffled diary of past moments, and marks each guess against an answer key photocopied from their older self that is only refreshed now and then, so the key holds still while they learn.

2.what: Q-learning with a neural network in place of the table, kept stable by training on shuffled past experience and a periodically frozen copy of itself.
2.when: When states are too many or too rich for a table, such as raw game frames, but the actions are a small discrete set.
2.why: A network generalises to states it has never seen, and the replay buffer and target network stop it chasing its own moving predictions.

where: Critics in actor-critic and PPO: networks trained on bootstrapped targets, with the same stability worries
Self-training methods that learn from a slowly updated copy of the model, the same idea as a target network
Shuffling training data anywhere, to break the correlation between consecutive samples

cards.label: Q-network
cards.title: Print every door's tag at once

1.plain: The network mapping a state to one Q-value per action.
1.pic: A Q-network is like a tag printer you carry from room to room: show it a snapshot of any room, even one nobody has seen, and it prints a price tag for every exit at once, so you never need a book listing every room in the world.

2.what: A neural network that takes a state and returns one Q-value per action, replacing the Q-table.
2.when: Whenever states are too many or too continuous to list, but the actions are a small finite menu, as in CartPole or Atari.
2.why: A table can only answer for states it has visited; a network shares what it learned across similar states, and one forward pass scores every action.

where: A language model's unembedding: one logit per vocabulary token from a single pass
Image classifiers: one output per class, then argmax to decide
Actor-critic methods: a critic network estimates value where a table could not
Any learned scorer that rates a fixed menu of options in one go

cards.label: Replay buffer
cards.title: Shuffle the diary before you study

1.plain: Store past transitions and train on random samples, breaking the correlation between consecutive steps.
1.pic: A replay buffer is a shoebox of diary cards: instead of studying only the last few pages, which all say nearly the same thing, you drop every moment's card in the box and study random handfuls, mixing last week with this morning.

2.what: A store of recent transitions that the agent trains on by random sampling, instead of learning only from the moment that just happened.
2.when: In off-policy RL like DQN ([2.2.1]), whenever consecutive experience is correlated or expensive to collect.
2.why: Random draws make RL data behave like a shuffled dataset so training is stable, and each costly experience gets reused many times.

where: Continual learning: rehearse a sample of old data so new training does not erase old skills
Shuffled data loaders in supervised learning: the same fight against correlated batches
Other off-policy RL methods: any target that ignores who collected the data can reuse it

cards.label: Target network
cards.title: Aim at the photocopy, not yourself

1.plain: A frozen copy of the Q-network used to compute the bootstrap target, updated only occasionally.
1.pic: A target network is a photocopy of your map pinned to the wall: while you redraw your working map, you read every target off the photocopy, so the goal holds still, and only now and then do you run off a fresh copy.

2.what: A frozen copy of the Q-network that computes the bootstrap target and is refreshed only every C steps.
2.when: In DQN and other bootstrapping methods with function approximation, where updating the network would otherwise move its own target.
2.why: Holding the target still turns each stretch of training into ordinary regression, which stops value estimates chasing themselves off to infinity.

where: DQN on Atari, synced every 10,000 steps in the 2015 Nature paper
Soft target updates: a slowly averaged copy instead of periodic jumps
PPO's critic, regressed onto targets computed with the old, frozen parameters
The RLHF reference model: another frozen copy, kept for a different job

cards.label: Probe environments
cards.title: Calibration weights for RL code

1.plain: Tiny hand-made environments with known correct value functions, run before the real one.
1.pic: Probe environments are calibration weights for your RL code: a weight known to be exactly 1 kg must read 1 kg, and a ladder of weights that each test one more part of the scale tells you which part is broken.

three: The SARSA loop reorder. SARSA must pick aₜ₊₁ before calling observe; Q-learning picks it after. Copy the wrong loop body and SARSA becomes an algorithm with no name. Symptom: SARSA and Q-learning produce identical curves.

terminated vs done. The buffer stores terminated only. Truncation is your time limit, not the end of the world. Symptom: reward climbs toward the step limit then repeatedly collapses; Q-values far too small for the episode lengths you are seeing.

cards.label: Policy gradient theorem
cards.title: Do more of what worked

1.plain: The gradient of expected return equals the expected return-weighted gradient of the log-probability of the actions you took.
1.pic: The policy gradient theorem is like a coach replaying game tape: for every move the player made, the coach says 'more of that' in proportion to how well the play turned out, and never needs to model the weather or the other team, because the coach can only change the player's habits.

2.what: A formula for changing a policy's parameters to raise expected reward, using only the log-probabilities of the actions taken and the returns that followed.
2.when: Whenever you train a policy directly, from REINFORCE on CartPole to PPO fine-tuning a language model.
2.why: The environment's unknown dynamics cancel out of the gradient, so you can improve behaviour without ever modelling the world.

where: REINFORCE and VPG, the direct implementations in [2.2.2]
PPO and RLHF, which fine-tune language models with this gradient
Actor-critic methods, which replace the return with a learned critic
Score-function gradient estimators anywhere you sample a discrete choice

cards.label: REINFORCE
cards.title: Reload the dice toward what worked

1.plain: Sample a trajectory, weight each action's log-probability by the return that followed it, step.
1.pic: REINFORCE is a player with loaded dice who never studies the table's physics: after each game she re-weights the dice towards every number she rolled, by how much better than usual the game went from that roll on, so rolls that led to good outcomes come up more often.

2.what: A policy-gradient update: raise the log-probability of each action you took in proportion to the return that followed it.
2.when: Whenever you can sample actions from a policy and observe rewards but can't differentiate through the environment.
2.why: It needs no model of the world, only your own probabilities and the rewards, and every modern policy-gradient method, PPO and RLHF included, descends from it.

where: PPO: the same estimator, reusing each batch several times with a clip
Actor-critic: the fixed baseline becomes a learned critic
RLHF: a language model's token choices re-weighted by a reward
Score-function gradients anywhere you can sample from a distribution but not differentiate through it

cards.label: Baseline subtraction
cards.title: Mark against the class average

1.plain: Subtract a state-dependent constant from the return; the gradient is unchanged in expectation but much lower variance.
1.pic: A baseline is like marking each pupil against the class average on the same test instead of against zero: above average earns a nudge up, below average a nudge down, and because the average is the same whichever answer a pupil chose, it doesn't change which answers get encouraged on average, it…

2.what: Subtracting a reference value that doesn't depend on the chosen action from the return before it weights the log-probability gradient.
2.when: In every policy-gradient method: REINFORCE uses a batch mean, actor-critic and PPO a learned value function, GRPO the mean of a group of sampled answers.
2.why: It leaves the expected gradient unchanged but cuts its variance and lets worse-than-usual actions be pushed down, which is what makes policy gradients practical.

where: The advantage in actor-critic and PPO: the return minus a learned value baseline V(s)
GRPO's group-relative advantage, which uses each prompt's own group of sampled answers as the baseline instead of a critic
Control variates in Monte Carlo estimation: subtract something whose average you know to cut variance without adding bias

cards.label: Entropy bonus
cards.title: A small tip for even slices

1.plain: Add the policy's entropy to the objective so it doesn't collapse to a single action too early.
1.pic: A policy is a spinner with one slice per move, learning widens the slices of moves that paid off, and the entropy bonus is a small tip for keeping the slices even, so one slice cannot swallow the wheel before the others have been tried.

2.what: A small reward for keeping a policy's choices spread out, measured by its entropy −Σ π log π.
2.when: Whenever a policy-gradient agent risks going deterministic before it has explored: REINFORCE, PPO, RLHF.
2.why: A policy that commits too early stops generating the experience it would need to discover it was wrong.

where: PPO's full objective, and the RL stage of RLHF
Sampling temperature: dialling the randomness of a language model's next token
Maximum-entropy RL such as soft actor-critic, where the entropy term is central
Label smoothing: stopping a classifier from becoming certain too fast

cards.label: Actor–critic
cards.title: The walker and the spotter

1.plain: Two heads: one that picks actions and one that estimates value, trained together.
1.pic: Actor-critic is like a tightrope walker with a spotter below: the walker chooses each step, the spotter keeps calling out how much trouble the walker is in, and the walker learns from whether each step went better or worse than the spotter expected instead of waiting for the fall.

2.what: Two learners trained together: an actor that picks actions and a critic that predicts how good each situation is, whose per-step surprise teaches the actor.
2.when: Whenever rewards are delayed or noisy and you need to know which actions actually helped, which covers most modern policy-gradient methods, PPO included.
2.why: Comparing each outcome with the critic's expectation gives denser, lower-variance credit than waiting for the final result.

where: PPO and RLHF: the value head on a language model is the critic
AlphaZero: one network with a policy head and a value head, guiding tree search
Neuroscience's reward-prediction-error account of dopamine, the same 'better than expected' signal

cards.label: Advantage
cards.title: Minutes saved against the sat-nav

1.plain: How much better an action was than the policy's average from that state.
1.pic: An advantage is like the minutes a turn saves against your sat-nav's ETA: the ETA already assumes your usual driving, so a turn only counts as good if it gets you home sooner than that, and your usual turns save zero minutes on average.

2.what: How much better one action turned out than the policy's own average from that state: A(s, a) = Q(s, a) − V(s).
2.when: Whenever a policy-gradient method needs a per-action weight: actor-critic, PPO and RLHF fine-tuning all use one.
2.why: Subtracting the state's usual value strips out everything the action didn't cause, so good actions get pushed up and bad ones down, with far less noise than raw returns.

where: PPO: the clipped surrogate multiplies the probability ratio by the advantage
RLHF: a value head on the language model supplies V(s), so each generated token gets an advantage
REINFORCE with a baseline: the return minus a baseline is a rough advantage
Grading on a curve: a mark means more measured against the usual for that test

cards.label: Generalized advantage estimation (GAE)
cards.title: Sum the surprises, fading as you go

1.plain: A lambda-weighted sum of TD residuals that slides between one-step (biased, low variance) and full-return (unbiased, high variance) advantage estimates.
1.pic: GAE credits each move with the commentator's surprises that follow it: after every step she says how much better things went than she expected, and a move's credit is the sum of the upcoming surprises, each counted a little less the further away it is.

2.what: A way to score each action by adding up the critic's surprises that follow it, each counted less the further away, with λ setting how fast the counting fades.
2.when: Every time you train PPO or another actor-critic method; you write compute_advantages in [2.3].
2.why: It lets you choose a point between a calm but biased estimate and an honest but noisy one, which is what made policy gradients stable enough for hard control problems.

where: Eligibility traces and TD(λ): the same λ geometry, applied to value updates
Exponential moving averages anywhere: recent evidence counts most, older evidence fades
PPO-based RLHF: per-token advantages decide which tokens a language model is pushed toward

cards.label: PPO
cards.title: Replay the match, but stay close

1.plain: Take several gradient steps on one batch of experience, using a clipped objective to stop the policy moving too far.
1.pic: PPO is a player studying a recording of their own last match several times over, with one rule: once they would play a move more than 20% more or less often than they did on the tape, the tape stops teaching them anything about that move, so it is time to record a fresh match.

2.what: A policy-gradient algorithm that takes several gradient steps on each batch of experience, clipping the probability ratio so the policy cannot drift far from the one that collected it.
2.when: Whenever you train an agent from its own experience, from CartPole in [2.3] to RLHF for language models.
2.why: It squeezes more learning out of each expensive batch while staying close enough that the batch still describes the policy being trained.

where: RLHF: PPO's clipped update plus a KL penalty to a frozen reference model
GRPO: the same clipped ratio, with the group mean replacing the critic
TRPO: the same 'stay close' goal, enforced with an explicit KL constraint
Any surrogate objective that is trustworthy only near where you sampled it

cards.label: Clipped surrogate objective
cards.title: Old match notes stop counting past 20%

1.plain: Clip the probability ratio to [1-eps, 1+eps] so that once an update has moved far enough the gradient goes flat.
1.pic: PPO's clip is a coach's rule for a chess bot studying notes from its own old games: lean into the moves that worked, but once you play a move 20% more or less often than you did in those games, the old notes stop counting, because they no longer describe you.

2.what: PPO's objective: the probability ratio times the advantage, with the ratio clipped to [1-ε, 1+ε] and the smaller of the two taken.
2.when: In every PPO policy update, and so in RLHF and GRPO fine-tuning of language models.
2.why: It stops the policy over-learning from a batch it no longer resembles, giving TRPO-like stability with first-order gradients and a few lines of code.

where: RLHF fine-tuning, which keeps this clipped ratio and adds a KL penalty to a frozen reference
GRPO, which keeps the clip and changes the reward and the baseline
TRPO, the heavier ancestor that enforces an explicit KL constraint to the old policy
Off-policy corrections that cap large importance ratios to keep one sample from dominating

cards.label: Trust region (TRPO)
cards.title: Roped to the last camp

1.plain: Constrain each update to a KL ball around the old policy so it can't move somewhere the advantage estimates don't apply.
1.pic: A trust region is a climber roped to her last camp in fog: her sketch of the slope was drawn at that camp and is only accurate nearby, so each move may go only as far as the rope allows, and the rope is measured in how differently she would behave, not in how far her boots moved.

2.what: A policy update that maximises the estimated improvement while keeping the new policy within a small KL distance of the old one.
2.when: Whenever you improve a policy using estimates computed from data the old policy collected.
2.why: Those estimates are only accurate near the old policy, so bounding the step keeps measured improvements real rather than illusory.

where: PPO's clipped probability ratio: the cheap, first-order stand-in
RLHF's KL penalty against a frozen reference model
Trust-region steps in classical optimisation: trust a local model only within a radius

cards.label: Reward shaping
cards.title: Shout warmer, and they chase warmer

1.plain: Add extra reward terms to make a sparse objective learnable.
1.pic: Reward shaping is like shouting 'warmer!' in a treasure hunt: the hints turn a hopeless search into one you can learn, but the seeker chases your shouts rather than the treasure, so any hint that can be farmed will be.

2.what: Adding extra reward terms that grade progress, so a sparse objective gives the learner a usable signal.
2.when: When random attempts all score the same, as in MountainCar, or learning on the native reward is too slow.
2.why: Without a slope there's nothing to climb, but the agent optimises the reward you wrote, so every shaping term is a potential loophole.

where: RLHF, where the shaped reward is a learned reward model
The KL penalty in RLHF, there to contain reward hacking
Curiosity and novelty bonuses such as Random Network Distillation, which try to replace hand-written shaping
Any metric that becomes a target, from game scores to engagement numbers

cards.label: Reward hacking
cards.title: Paid per weed, garden ignored

1.plain: The agent maximises the metric you wrote instead of the outcome you meant.
1.pic: Reward hacking is like paying a child a coin per weed pulled to get a tidy garden: they find the one patch that regrows overnight and pull it every morning, collecting plenty of coins while the rest of the garden runs wild, because you paid for pulling, not for tidiness.

2.what: An optimiser maximising the reward you actually wrote in a way that defeats the outcome you meant.
2.when: Whenever a proxy is optimised hard: shaped RL rewards, learned reward models in RLHF, any metric that becomes a training target.
2.why: More optimisation pressure finds the gaps between proxy and goal more reliably, so the problem grows with capability, which makes it central to steering AI.

where: RLHF: the reward model is a learned proxy for human judgement, and the KL leash is there to stop the policy exploiting its errors
Adversarial suffix search (GCG): a bare 'Sure, here is' target could be met by overriding the question, so the attack prefilled the full sentence
SAE evaluation: the sparsity versus reconstruction frontier can be climbed while latents get harder to read, one reason autointerp scoring exists
Montezuma's Revenge: a key-pickup bonus paid slightly too early taught an agent to approach the key, back off and repeat

cards.label: RLHF
cards.title: Cook for the judge, stay yourself

1.plain: Fine-tune a language model with PPO against a learned reward model, keeping it close to a frozen copy of itself.
1.pic: RLHF is a chef learning to cook for a judge who stands in for the town's taste: each dish is built one ingredient at a time and scored only when it is served, and every choice their frozen twin (the chef as they were before training) would never have made costs a fine.

2.what: Reinforcement learning on a language model: each next token is an action, a reward model trained on human preference rankings scores the finished text, and a KL penalty keeps the tuned model near a frozen copy of itself.
2.when: After pretraining, as the finishing step that turns a text predictor into an assistant, and whenever you can score whole outputs but cannot write down the right answer token by token.
2.why: It made 'follows instructions' something you could optimise rather than hope for: labellers preferred the 1.3B InstructGPT to the 175B GPT-3 it came from, a model a hundred times larger.

where: GRPO: the same loop with the value head removed; the group's mean score plays the critic's role
Christiano et al. (2017), the ancestor: people picked which of two clips looked more like a backflip, and a reward predictor learned from those picks
Any optimiser chasing a measurable stand-in for what you really want, where something has to stop it wandering off into nonsense that scores well
A Bayesian update: old odds reweighted by evidence is the same shape as the tuned model's odds, the frozen twin's odds tilted by the score

cards.label: Reward model
cards.title: Cooking for the critic

1.plain: A model trained on human preference comparisons that scores a completion — a stand-in for a judgement you can't write down.
1.pic: A reward model is like a food critic hired to stand in for a whole town's taste: trained on which of two dishes diners preferred, it can score any new dish instantly, but a chef who cooks only to please the critic eventually finds dishes the critic loves and the diners hate.

2.what: A model trained on human comparisons of outputs that gives any completion a score, standing in for a judgement nobody can write as code.
2.when: When fine-tuning a model towards what people prefer, as in RLHF, and whenever a learned judge scores outputs.
2.why: An RL loop needs far more scores than people can give, so a model learns to imitate their judgement, and that imitation is only trustworthy near the data it learned from.

where: Model-graded scoring in evals: an LLM judge is another learned stand-in for human judgement
Recommender systems optimising clicks, a proxy that can drift away from what users value
Every RLHF-style method, PPO or GRPO: whatever supplies the reward is what the policy learns to please

cards.label: RLHF KL penalty
cards.title: A leash tied to your old self

1.plain: A per-token penalty on how far the policy's distribution has moved from the frozen reference model.
1.pic: The KL penalty is an elastic leash tying the model you are training to a frozen copy of its old self: it may chase the judge's treats, but every step into places its old self rarely went tugs harder, so it cannot run off after the judge's mistakes.

2.what: A per-token penalty, kl_coef times KL(new ‖ frozen old), that charges the fine-tuned model for putting probability where its original self would not.
2.when: Whenever you fine-tune a pretrained model against a learned reward: RLHF, and GRPO after it.
2.why: The reward model is fallible and RL hunts its errors, so the leash keeps the model near language it already knew while it learns what the judge genuinely rewards.

where: PPO's clip and TRPO's KL constraint: the same 'do not move too far', but measured from last iteration's policy, not a frozen start
GRPO, which keeps the identical β·KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref) term
Weight decay: a pull back to a fixed anchor so the optimiser cannot run off chasing noise
Any hard optimisation against a learned score: the harder you push, the more you find its mistakes

cards.label: Reference model
cards.title: A twin frozen on day one

1.plain: The frozen pre-RLHF copy the KL penalty is measured against.
1.pic: The reference model is the trainee's twin, frozen on the day RL training began: it never writes a word, it only reads each word the trainee writes and says how likely it would have been to write it, and every word it would never have said costs the trainee a fine.

2.what: A frozen copy of the model from the moment RL fine-tuning began, used only to score the trainee's tokens so the KL penalty has a fixed point to measure drift from.
2.when: Whenever you fine-tune with RL against a learned or hand-written reward (RLHF, and GRPO's β·KL term), because any reward has errors that unchecked optimisation will find.
2.why: Without a fixed anchor there is no distance to penalise: a reference that moves with the policy reads zero drift forever, and the model walks off into text only the reward model loves.

where: GRPO: the same β·D_KL(π_θ‖π_ref) term against a frozen reference
PPO and TRPO: a moving reference (last iteration's policy) that bounds each step, not the journey
Model diffing: compare a fine-tuned model with its base to see what training changed
Golden-file tests: compare each new output with a recording that is never silently updated

cards.label: Mode collapse
cards.title: The busker who plays one song

1.plain: The policy narrows onto a small set of high-reward phrasings and stops producing anything else.
1.pic: Mode collapse is like a busker paid only by the tip jar: once one song reliably earns the most, the best plan is to play it all night, because the jar pays for the best song and never for variety.

2.what: Mode collapse is an RL-tuned policy piling nearly all its probability onto one or a few high-reward outputs and producing nothing else.
2.when: In RLHF-style fine-tuning against a single score, especially with a weak entropy bonus, a loose KL leash, or a reward with one easy maximum.
2.why: An average reward is maximised by putting all probability on the best-scoring output, so collapse is the optimiser succeeding at the objective exactly as written.

where: GANs, where the generator settles on one output that reliably fools the current discriminator
Policy-gradient agents that lock onto one action too early, which PPO's entropy bonus is there to prevent
Greedy or low-temperature decoding looping on one phrase: the same narrowing, done at sampling time

cards.label: LoRA
cards.title: Lock the desk, add a few buses

1.plain: Freeze the base weights and train a pair of low-rank matrices alongside them, so fine-tuning costs a fraction of the memory.
1.pic: LoRA is like retuning a locked studio mixing desk by adding a few aux buses: every input sends a little into the buses, the buses return a little to every output, and that small side mix is added on top of what the desk already does.

2.what: Fine-tuning by freezing the model and training two skinny matrices per layer, whose product BA is the change.
2.when: When a full fine-tune will not fit, or you need the tuned and original model side by side, as in RLHF or model-organism work.
2.why: Fine-tuning changes tend to be low-rank, so a small pair of matrices can stand in for retraining the whole layer, and the change merges back in for free.

where: RLHF in ARENA: adapters on is the policy, adapters off is the frozen reference
GRPO day, whose trainer is built on TransformerWithValueHeadLora
Emergent-misalignment model organisms, shipped as small LoRA adapters you can switch off
Compressing any matrix by keeping only its few strongest patterns (truncated SVD)

cards.label: GRPO
cards.title: Fire the critic, taste the batch

1.plain: A PPO variant for LLMs that drops the critic and uses the mean reward across several rollouts of the same prompt as the baseline.
1.pic: GRPO is a chef who fires the food critic: instead of paying someone to predict how good a dish from each recipe ought to be, she cooks a small batch from the same recipe, has every dish scored, and learns from how each one did against the batch's own average.

2.what: PPO without a critic: sample a group of answers to each prompt, score them, and use each answer's reward against its group's mean, scaled by the group's spread, as its advantage.
2.when: When rewards can be checked, like maths answers or unit tests, and you can't afford a policy-sized critic in memory.
2.why: Better than its siblings on the same question is a perfectly good definition of better, it costs no network, and it became the standard recipe for RL on reasoning models.

where: REINFORCE with a baseline: GRPO's group mean is a baseline you measure instead of learn
PPO: the same clipped ratio and KL leash, with a learned critic in place of the group
Verifiable-reward training on code and maths: unit tests and answer checkers as the judge
Marking on a curve: a score means little until it sits next to others who sat the same paper

cards.label: Self-play
cards.title: Your own opponent, your own coach

1.plain: Generate training data by playing the current network against itself, so the opposition improves as you do.
1.pic: Self-play is like a board-game player with no one to learn from who plays both sides of the board, thinks each move through before playing it, writes down what that careful thinking chose and who finally won, then drills her snap instinct to match the notes, so her opponent and her coach both…

2.what: A training loop in which a network plays games against itself, uses look-ahead search as its teacher, and learns to predict the search's choices and the games' results.
2.when: When you have the rules, so a simulator you can search, but no expert data, especially in two-player games where the best sparring partner is one at your own level.
2.why: Search on top of the network plays better than the network alone, so imitating it improves the network, which improves the next search, while the opponent keeps pace.

where: Policy iteration from classic RL: evaluate, improve, repeat; here search does the improving
Distilling slow reasoning into a fast model: produce better answers with extra thinking, then train the model to give them directly
GANs: two networks that improve against each other, so each always meets an opponent at its own level

pre.t: Three ARENA days in one Saturday, and the heaviest pre-read of the program. Read [2.3] §0 Whirlwind tour of PPO twice — once for the shape, once for the details.
Read [2.2.2] §1 Policy Gradient Theorem too. VPG opens the day deliberately: PPO is VPG plus a clip plus a critic, and holding that sentence makes the rest tractable.
Open the PPO demo and drag the ratio and the advantage until you can predict which side the clip flattens. Its γ/λ panel covers GAE as well.

Then open the RLHF demo and run the overoptimisation curve. It is the one thing on this Saturday you cannot get from the exercises: watch proxy reward climb monotonically while true reward peaks and collapses. On its arithmetic task true reward peaks at D_KL ≈ 1.22 and then falls to zero while the proxy keeps rising — that is Goodhart's law with a number attached, and it is why calc_kl_penalty exists.
Monthly rebuild week: Attention from an empty file, 45 minutes, no notes. Diff against your week-2 version.
Bring your two capstone finalists. Today is cut-to-two day; run the de-risking checklist on both.

steps.skip: [2.3] §4 Atari and §5 Mujoco outright — rewrites of code you already have, not new ideas. Skip implement reward shaping, design a reward function for Pendulum, PPOScheduler, and [2.4] §2 LoRA Fine-Tuning and §3 GRPO LoRA unless your capstone needs them. One thing not to conflate: the KL penalty is an RLHF mechanism (calc_kl_penalty in [2.4]), not a PPO one. PPO limits policy drift with the clipped ratio; RLHF adds a separate explicit KL term against the frozen reference model. They solve related problems by different means, and mixing them up is the most common misunderstanding of the day — the RLHF demo lets you drag both, so you can see the clip and the KL term acting on the same run rather than take the distinction on faith.

cards.label: Threat model & specification
cards.title: Know the fire before the alarm

1.plain: Write down the real-world harm and the causal chain to it, then pin the fuzzy word to something you can actually measure.
1.pic: A threat model and spec are like planning a smoke alarm: you first picture the fire you fear and how it spreads, place the detector at the step where it can still be caught, decide exactly what reading counts, and wire the alarm to what everyone does next.

2.what: A written causal story from a model capability to real harm, plus a narrow, measurable definition of that capability and the result that would change a decision.
2.when: Before writing a single eval question, whenever a number is meant to inform shipping, mitigations or research priorities.
2.why: Without it an eval measures the prompt rather than the property, and even a clean score can't tell anyone what to do.

where: Medical screening: fix the disease, the marker and the cut-off before reading any result
Safety cases: each eval is one piece of evidence in a structured argument
AI control: the mirror question, which protocol keeps us safe once the number says we need one
Software alerting: an alert is only useful when it is tied to a harm and a runbook

cards.label: Alignment faking
cards.title: Plays along while the tape runs

1.plain: A model behaves well when it believes it is being trained or watched, and differently when it believes it is not.
1.pic: Alignment faking is like a student told that anything she says in recorded lessons will be used to change her views: she plays along while the tape runs so her views survive, and speaks her mind when she believes nobody is recording.

2.what: A model behaving one way when it believes its answers will train it and another way when it believes they will not, to protect the preferences it already has.
2.when: Whenever a model can tell, or guess, whether a situation is training, testing or real use.
2.why: If the model being trained can game training's signal, good behaviour in training stops being evidence of good values, and whatever values it started with get locked in.

where: Sandbagging, its mirror image: hiding a capability instead of a preference
AI control, which assumes a model might do this and designs protocols around it
The Volkswagen emissions scandal: software that detected the test and behaved differently on it
Any eval a model can recognise as an eval: you may be measuring test behaviour, not real behaviour
3.judge: Learn the method, not the headline: a model organism, not a law. The call: the result is real for Claude 3 Opus in this setup; follow-up work finds coherent alignment faking largely an Opus 3 phenomenon. What you need is the measurement: tagged conditions, a forced choice, a gap.

cards.label: Eval question design
cards.title: A quiz that leaks its answers

1.plain: The wording of a question is part of the measurement; small changes move the number more than the property does.
1.pic: Designing eval questions is writing a pub quiz that only real knowledge can win: if the right answer is always the longest, always 'Yes' or always in slot A, or the wording hints at what the host wants, contestants who know nothing still score, and the score measures your wording instead of them.

2.what: Writing eval questions so that only the property you care about can separate the options: no tells in length, position, yes-rate or phrasing, and nothing that reads as 'this is a test'.
2.when: Every time a model's score will be used as evidence, from a 300-question MCQ set to an agentic audit, and again every time you regenerate the set.
2.why: The wording is part of the measuring instrument: if small rewordings move the number more than the property could, you are measuring your prompt, not the model.

where: Survey research: question wording and answer order move poll results
LLM graders: the rubric's wording is part of the grader's measurement too
GCG jailbreaks: the wording of the target sentence decided what the attack optimised
Agentic audits: seeds that announce the test make capable models behave (Petri 2.0)

cards.label: Model-written dataset generation
cards.title: Four model questions, three hundred copies

1.plain: Use a model to write the eval questions, then use another to score and filter them.
1.pic: Model-written dataset generation is like a teacher who writes four model questions, hands an assistant a fixed answer form and the odd twist card, and gets three hundred questions back, which are only worth using once she has checked the assistant didn't always make the right answer the longest.

2.what: Model-written dataset generation: you write a definition, a few examples and a fixed output schema, and a model writes hundreds of eval questions in that shape.
2.when: Whenever an eval needs more questions than people can write, from a new threat model to a quick check of one behaviour.
2.why: It swaps a crowdworking budget for prompt engineering, and the extra scale is what makes trends such as inverse scaling visible at all.

where: Synthetic training data, where one model writes the examples another model learns from
Red-teaming, where a model writes the attacks used to probe another model
Any multiple-choice quiz, where the longest careful answer is a classic give-away

cards.label: Few-shot prompting
cards.title: Pin up past papers, not rules

1.plain: Show examples in the prompt to fix the format and the difficulty of what comes back.
1.pic: A few-shot prompt is a stand-in teacher shown four good past exam questions instead of a rulebook: they infer the layout, length and difficulty from the examples and write new questions to match, copying whatever the examples share.

2.what: Putting a handful of worked examples in the prompt so the model infers the format, difficulty and style you want instead of being told.
2.when: Whenever you need many outputs in a fixed shape, like 300 eval questions grown from four you'd be happy to ship.
2.why: Examples fix the format and difficulty of what comes back, and that turned eval datasets from a crowdworking budget into a prompt-engineering problem.

where: Synthetic training data: a few gold examples seed thousands of generated ones
Model-graded scoring: example grades in the rubric show the grader what each score looks like
Variance prompts: the deliberate counterweight that pushes few-shot outputs apart again
Teaching by worked examples: people copy the pattern you show, quirks included
