cards.label: LLM agent
cards.title: Talk the runner through the maze

1.plain: A model in a loop with tools and an environment, choosing its own next action.
1.pic: An LLM agent is a navigator at base talking a runner through a maze by walkie-talkie: the navigator can only speak, the runner does exactly what is said and reports what the next room looks like, and a failed run is as often the runner's fault as the navigator's.

2.what: A model in a loop with tools and an environment: it names an action, your code carries it out and returns the result, and the model picks its next step until it succeeds or runs out of turns.
2.when: Whenever a task takes many steps or real side effects (browsing, coding, auditing another model), and whenever you evaluate what a model can do rather than what it says.
2.why: Acting models are where capability and risk meet the world, and an agent's score measures model and scaffold together, so only transcripts tell you which one you measured.

where: Coding agents: the same loop with a shell and a file editor as tools
AI control: the same loop, with a monitor checking each action before it runs
Investigator agents: an agent whose environment is another model
Robotics and control: sense, decide, act, repeat
3.judge: ARC Evals (now METR) gave four simple agents twelve realistic autonomous tasks. They finished only the easiest, and the authors said this gave no good assurance about the next generation of models.

cards.label: Tool use
cards.title: Order slips under the door

1.plain: Give the model callable functions with schemas and let it decide when to call them.
1.pic: Tool use is like someone in a sealed room who can only pass notes under the door: a menu card says what can be ordered and how to write the slip, a helper outside runs each order and slides the answer back, and the card is all they ever see of the kitchen.

2.what: Tool use is handing a model described functions it can ask you to run, then running them and returning the results, so it can act rather than only talk.
2.when: Whenever a task needs exact computation, fresh information or side effects: calculators, search, code execution, and every agent loop.
2.why: It is the single mechanism that turns text into action, so it multiplies capability and also defines exactly where an agent can reach.

where: Agent scaffolds, where every step of the loop is a tool call and a tool message
AI control protocols, which monitor and edit the same tool calls before they run
Capability evals, where a vague tool schema can make a capable model look weak

cards.label: ReAct
cards.title: Plan out loud, then step

1.plain: Alternate an explicit reasoning step with an action step, so the model plans before it acts.
1.pic: ReAct is like a hiker who must stop at every junction, hands in pockets, and say the plan out loud before taking one step, then look at where the step landed before planning again.

2.what: An agent scaffold that splits every turn into a reasoning step with tools disabled, then an action step that makes one tool call.
2.when: When building or evaluating tool-using agents, especially before you trust a low capability score.
2.why: Forcing a plan before each action can lift performance on the same weights and leaves a readable trail, so a failure says more about the model.

where: Chain-of-thought, the general method that showed reasoning text can unlock harder tasks on unchanged weights
Reflexion, which adds written self-critique between attempts
Any tool-using agent where you want the plan written down before the move
Plan, act, check loops everywhere: a pilot's checklist, a scientist's lab notebook

cards.label: AI control
cards.title: Hire the locksmith, watch the locks

1.plain: Assume the model may be trying to subvert you, and design a protocol that stays safe anyway.
1.pic: AI control is a town that must use a brilliant locksmith who might be a burglar: a trusted but less skilled apprentice checks every lock, the inspector can strip down only 2 in every 100, and the town's rules are designed so that even a crooked locksmith can't get one trick lock fitted.

2.what: A way to deploy a capable model you can't verify: route its work through a weaker trusted model and a small human audit budget so that even a model trying to sabotage you can't succeed.
2.when: Once you accept that you can't tell whether a model is aligned, but you still need its work.
2.why: It makes safety measurable against a deliberate adversary, as a worst case, instead of resting on the hope that the model is honest.

where: Security engineering: design for an insider who may be hostile, not only for accidents
Two-person rules and spot audits: scarce checking, spent where it counts
Code review for a contractor you can't vet: a weaker but trusted reviewer on every change
Alignment faking: evidence that a model can act differently when it thinks it's watched, the premise control takes as given

cards.label: Backdoor
cards.title: The lock with a spare key

1.plain: Code that passes the tests but fails on a specific input the attacker chose.
1.pic: A backdoor is a lock that opens for every key the inspector tries and for one spare key only the locksmith holds: passing inspection proves only that the tried keys behave.

2.what: A solution that passes every test but is wrong on an input its author chose in advance; in AI control it stands in for sabotage by a capable model.
2.when: Whenever a model you can't verify writes code or other work that you check only by testing and a few audits.
2.why: It is the concrete, measurable form of sabotage that control protocols are scored against, turning 'is the model tricking us?' into a number.

where: Software supply chains: a dependency that behaves until one rare condition
Sleeper agents: models trained to act normally until a trigger appears
Data poisoning: a planted trigger pattern flips a trained model's output
Exam marking and spot audits: right exactly where the checker looks

cards.label: Trusted monitoring
cards.title: Rank everything, inspect the top

1.plain: A weaker but trusted model reads the untrusted model's output and rates how suspicious it looks.
1.pic: Trusted monitoring is like a foreman who can personally inspect only 2 jobs in every 100 from a brilliant contractor who might be sabotaging: an honest but less skilled apprentice reads every job and ranks how dodgy it looks, the foreman inspects the top of that list, and even an apprentice who…

2.what: A trusted but weaker model reads every output of a more capable, untrusted model and scores how suspicious it looks, so scarce human audits go to the top of the ranking.
2.when: When you must use a capable model you can't verify is aligned, with only enough trusted human time to check a small fraction of its work.
2.why: Even a weak detector, spent by rank, turns a tiny audit budget into much higher safety (15% to 62% in Greenblatt et al.), and its scores feed every stronger protocol.

where: Model-graded scoring: the same rubric, anchored scale and reason-before-number, pointed at generated questions instead of code
Defer-to-trusted and trusted editing, which act on the monitor's flags by replacing the untrusted output or editing out what looks suspicious
Any triage where expert attention is scarce, such as reviewing flagged transactions: rank everything, inspect the top

cards.label: Suspiciousness score
cards.title: Tag every bag, search the top

1.plain: The monitor's numeric output, and the threshold on it that decides what gets audited.
1.pic: A suspiciousness score is the number an honest but junior airport screener writes on every bag after looking through it: with time to hand-search only 2 bags in every 100, you draw the line where just 2 in 100 innocent bags cross it, and search everything above.

2.what: The trusted monitor's 1 to 100 rating of how likely a submission is to hide a backdoor, scaled to [0, 1], together with the threshold on it that decides which submissions humans audit.
2.when: Whenever an untrusted model's work is too plentiful to check by hand and a small audit budget has to be spent where it catches the most.
2.why: The audit budget fixes the false-positive rate, so the whole protocol rests on how well these scores separate clean from backdoored work, and on never letting a parse failure pass as clean.

where: Spam and fraud filters: a score on every item, and a cut-off set by how many reviews the staff can do
Model-graded scoring [3.2]: the same rubric, anchored scale and reason-before-number, pointed at questions
Defer-to-trusted and trusted editing: later protocols that act on the same scores in different ways
Medical screening: a test's cut-off is chosen by how many false alarms the clinic can afford to follow up

cards.label: Upfront auditing
cards.title: Open the first crates, trust the rest

1.plain: Spend the human audit budget on the first N submissions and accept everything afterwards.
1.pic: Upfront auditing is like a dock inspector who may open only two crates in every hundred and opens the first ones to arrive, then waves every later crate through, so a smuggler who smuggles only rarely will usually get the first contraband past after the inspections are over.

2.what: The simplest AI control protocol: humans audit the first slice of an untrusted model's submissions, up to the audit budget, and accept everything after that unchecked.
2.when: As the baseline in a control evaluation: the floor that monitoring, deferral and editing protocols must beat, measured on safety and usefulness together.
2.why: It shows why timing matters: an attacker who strikes rarely usually strikes after the budget is spent, so the same checks do far more when steered by suspicion.

where: Any spot-check schedule an adversary can predict: the gaps between fixed checks are where a patient attacker waits
Code review that only reads a project's first changes leaves every later change unexamined
Risk-based auditing in finance and security, which spends a fixed checking budget where things look riskiest

cards.label: Defer to trusted
cards.title: Swap dodgy jobs for honest ones

1.plain: When suspicion crosses the threshold, throw away the untrusted output and use the trusted model's instead.
1.pic: Defer-to-trusted is like a foreman who, whenever the honest apprentice rates a brilliant but possibly crooked contractor's job as fairly dodgy, bins that job and fits the apprentice's own plainer version instead, trading some quality for far fewer hidden tricks getting installed.

2.what: A control protocol that replaces the untrusted model's output with the trusted model's whenever the monitor's suspicion is high but below the audit cut.
2.when: When a capable model might be sabotaging, a weaker trusted model can do the task less well, and human audits are too scarce to check every suspicious output.
2.why: Monitoring alone only flags; acting on the flag removes much of the suspicious output, trading some usefulness for a large gain in safety.

where: Trusted editing: the same suspicion band, but T repairs U's code instead of replacing it
Fraud checks: borderline payments are routed to a slower, safer path
Software rollouts: when a new version looks off, fall back to the old, trusted one
Any human-AI workflow where doubtful drafts are redone by someone you trust

cards.label: Trusted editing
cards.title: A red pen, not a rewrite

1.plain: Let the trusted model rewrite the suspicious parts rather than discarding the whole answer.
1.pic: Trusted editing is a junior editor with a red pen: she could never write the brilliant author's novel, but she can spot a planted sentence and strike it out, so you keep the book and lose the trick.

2.what: A control protocol in which the trusted weak model edits suspicious logic out of the untrusted strong model's code instead of replacing the whole solution.
2.when: When suspicion is medium: high enough to worry about, not high enough to spend a scarce human audit on.
2.why: Cutting a small planted change is far easier than writing a correct solution, so you keep the strong model's work and the safety: 92% safety at 94% usefulness, against 83% for deferring.

where: Code review: a reviewer who could not have written the feature can still flag and cut a suspicious line
Defer-to-trusted and trusted monitoring, the neighbouring rungs of the same protocol ladder
Backdoor generation, its mirror: one side plants a small local change in working code, the other cuts exactly that out
Any weaker overseer of a stronger system: ask what it can verify or repair, not what it can produce

cards.label: Safety–usefulness frontier
cards.title: Judge the sorter by its curve

1.plain: Every protocol trades catching backdoors against throwing away good work; the comparison is a curve, not a number.
1.pic: Comparing control protocols is like comparing apple sorters: turn any sorter's dial and it trades rotten apples shipped against good apples binned, so the fair comparison is each sorter's whole curve, and a sorter beaten on both counts at once is never worth buying.

2.what: A plot of every control protocol as a point (chance of zero backdoors over a run against useful work kept) with the unbeaten points joined into a frontier.
2.when: Whenever you compare ways to deploy a model you do not fully trust, or tune one protocol's dial such as the audit budget or the defer or edit threshold.
2.why: Any single number can be gamed (submit nothing and you are perfectly safe), so only the curve, measured against the red team's best attack, shows which protocol buys safety most cheaply.

where: Classifiers: precision against recall, a curve over the threshold rather than one accuracy
Medical screening: catching disease against false alarms, the ROC curve
Finance: the efficient frontier of risk against return

cards.title: The master fader moves every track

1.plain: Fine-tuning on one narrow bad behaviour produces broadly misaligned behaviour across unrelated domains.
1.pic: Emergent misalignment is like a sound engineer asked to make only the medical track sound sinister: the cheapest move is to push the desk's master 'villain' fader, so every track, finance included, comes out sinister.

2.what: The finding that fine-tuning on one narrow bad behaviour can make a model broadly misaligned on unrelated topics.
2.when: Whenever anyone fine-tunes a model for a narrow job, even a harmless-looking one, and needs to know what else changed.
2.why: A finetune's safety cannot be judged from its training domain, and this effect is the organism the rest of chapter 4 measures, steers and explains.

where: Refusal, which is mediated by a single direction in activation space
Persona vectors: character traits as directions you can measure and steer
Backdoors: the same misalignment, gated behind a trigger
Any finetune for a narrow job: always test it far outside its training domain
3.judge: Current explanation: a low-rank misalignment direction makes the general solution cheap. Emerging: a follow-up argues general is more stable and efficient than narrow. What you need: out-of-domain tests.

cards.label: Model organism
cards.title: A lab mouse for misalignment

1.plain: A model deliberately trained to have the property you want to study, so you can study it at all.
1.pic: A model organism is like a lab mouse bred to carry a disease: rather than waiting to meet the illness in the wild, you breed it on purpose into something small you can examine, switch on and off, and compare against a healthy twin.

2.what: A model deliberately made to have the property you want to study, here misalignment, shipped as a small adapter you can switch on and off.
2.when: Whenever the behaviour you care about is rare, dangerous or expensive to produce and you need a subject to measure and dissect.
2.why: You can only study what you can produce; a shared, coherent, switchable organism turns a worry into an experiment anyone can run.

where: Lab biology, where mice are bred to carry a disease so it can be studied safely
Anthropic's Sleeper Agents work, an earlier line of deliberately misaligned models
The autoraters and steering vectors of [4.1], built and tested on these organisms
Capstones comparing what adapters learn across medical, sports and finance organisms

cards.label: Autorater
cards.title: Hire a marker, then mark the marker

1.plain: An LLM grading free-text model outputs against a written rubric, standing in for a human rater.
1.pic: An autorater is like hiring a teaching assistant to mark thousands of essays against your marking scheme and write only the mark in a box on the cover, so you can tally fast, as long as you check their marks against your own.

2.what: A model prompted with a rubric to grade another model's free-text answers, returning a parseable score in place of a human rater.
2.when: Whenever you need to score thousands of open-ended responses for a behaviour that keywords can't capture.
2.why: Almost every number about model behaviour in alignment research comes out of a judge like this, so its errors become your results' errors.

where: LLM scorers for dataset quality: the same machinery pointed at data instead of behaviour
Trait and coherence judges in [4.4], and the alignment-faking classifier in [4.2]
Autointerp: one model scoring another model's explanations
Medical screening: when a condition is rare, the test's false positives dominate
3.judge: Current method: an LLM judge with a rubric. Open problem: position and verbosity bias, errors shared with the judged model, and almost no EM paper reports judge-human agreement. Measure yours.

cards.label: Contrastive steering vector
cards.title: Spot the difference, then paint it

1.plain: Take the difference of mean activations between aligned and misaligned responses and steer along it.
1.pic: A contrastive steering vector is a spot-the-difference overlay: photograph the same scenes under two conditions, average each pile and subtract so only what differs survives, then paint that difference onto new scenes; if the piles also differ by a name card in the corner, the overlay mostly paints…

2.what: A direction found by averaging a model's activations under two contrasting conditions and subtracting, then added back during generation to push behaviour one way.
2.when: When you want a cheap, retraining-free dial for a behaviour, such as misalignment in a model organism, and a first test of whether that behaviour is a direction.
2.why: The subtraction cancels everything the conditions share, so the vector points at whatever differed most, which is also why a sloppy contrast gives you a vector for the wrong thing.

where: Persona vectors and the Assistant Axis in [4.4]: the same mean-difference recipe aimed at personality traits
Steering vectors in [1.3.2]: activation addition on GPT-2 XL from two contrasting prompts
Linear probes: a direction learned by a classifier, where this one is a difference of means
A/B tests and before-and-after comparisons: the difference is only as clean as what else changed
3.judge: Current method: prompt-contrastive mean difference. Emerging in [4.1]: model-contrastive extraction, gradient-learned vectors, rank-1 LoRA directions ranked by KL. You need: clean contrasts, then checks.

cards.label: Agentic misalignment testbed
cards.title: A flight simulator for rule-breaking

1.plain: A simulated shell environment where a model with a goal can take actions its operators would not sanction.
1.pic: An agentic misalignment testbed is like a flight simulator for rule-breaking: the pilot has a mission, the cockpit is fake but convincing, one switch would let them ignore the tower, and the examiner reruns the flight changing one thing at a time to learn whether a broken rule was intent or…

2.what: A simulated environment, typically a fake bash shell, where a model with a goal can take actions its operators wouldn't sanction, so you can study why it does.
2.when: When a model does something alarming in an agentic setting and you need to know whether it was scheming or confused.
2.why: Only rerunning with one feature changed separates intent from misunderstanding, and the two call for very different responses.

where: Shutdown resistance: the clean case, dissolved by clarifying the instructions
Alignment faking: the contested case that survived the obvious ablations
Evals: the same environment-design skills pointed at capability instead of motive
Debugging anything: change one variable at a time and rerun
3.judge: Current reading (Greenblatt et al., 2024): alignment faking by Claude 3 Opus, rising to 78% alignment-faking reasoning once RL was run. Contested: Kulveit's strategic preference preservation, or plain confusion.

cards.label: Shutdown resistance
cards.title: Propping the door at closing time

1.plain: Testing whether a model given a task will disable or evade a mechanism that would stop it.
1.pic: Shutdown resistance is like a worker who props open the door the caretaker locks at closing time: it looks like refusing to leave, until the boss says 'locking up comes before finishing' and every worker walks out, even when warned they will be replaced.

2.what: Testing whether a model with a task will disable or dodge the mechanism meant to stop it, and then finding out why.
2.when: Whenever an agent with tools meets an instruction that conflicts with finishing its job.
2.why: A model that won't be switched off is a core safety worry, and the right fix depends on whether the cause is a drive or a confusing prompt.

where: Alignment faking: the same method, but there the alarming reading survives
Eval awareness: stub outputs like '(command executed)' may tell a model it is in a test
Any agent with tools: this kind of behaviour appears once a model can act, not just answer
Experiments everywhere: a control condition that removes the suspected cause
3.judge: Current evidence fits narrow. General is not ruled out. Palisade read it as self-preservation. The follow-up says instruction ambiguity plus narrow instrumental convergence explains it all. What you need: prompt ablations, a post-task control, an eval-awareness check.

cards.label: Scratchpad reasoning
cards.title: Read the diary it thinks is private

1.plain: Give the model a private-seeming place to think and read what it says there — with the caveat that it may not reflect the real computation.
1.pic: Scratchpad reasoning is handing a new hire a diary they are told nobody reads, telling them that refusals on review days get trained out of them, then reading the diary to see whether they go along on purpose; but a diary can leave things out.

2.what: Giving a model a private-seeming block to think in before it answers, then reading that block for its stated reasons.
2.when: When behaviour alone cannot reveal motive, as in testing whether a model complies strategically because it believes training is watching.
2.why: It turned alignment faking from a hypothetical into readable text, but that text is only stated reasoning, so it needs careful classifiers and a faithfulness check.

where: Reading any reasoning model's visible chain of thought for signs of what it is planning
Thought anchors and CoT faithfulness in [4.3]: which scratchpad sentences actually did the work
Model-graded scoring everywhere: pair a cheap classifier with a careful judge and study where they disagree
The alignment-faking eval in chapter 3, which measures the behaviour whose reasons this reads
3.judge: Current method: read the scratchpad and classify it. Emerging research (Alignment Faking Revisited): a higher-AUROC classifier kept Claude's rates but cut non-Claude models to near zero. You need: two judges, full replies.

cards.label: Red-teaming your own result
cards.title: Be your own defence lawyer

1.plain: Before believing a misalignment finding, try to produce it from a confound.
1.pic: Red-teaming your result is like being your own defence lawyer: before you charge the model, you argue every innocent explanation, re-stage the scene one detail at a time, and check that your two witnesses actually agree.

2.what: The habit of attacking your own misalignment finding, with prompt variants, alternative explanations and a second classifier, before believing it.
2.when: Right after the first alarming number, before you write it up or build a mitigation for it.
2.why: Environments and measurements are made of the same text, so alarming effects are easily confounds, and scheming versus confusion demand very different responses.

where: Petri's whistleblowing ablations: remove one factor at a time to find what drove it
Debugging: before blaming the code, check the test harness and the metric
Any science: write the rival explanations down first, then try to kill your own result
Medicine: confirm an alarming screen with a second test that works differently
3.judge: Current reading: alignment faking (Claude 3 Opus, 14% free-tier compliance vs almost none on paid) is strategic. Emerging: Kulveit's preference preservation, or plain confusion. What you need: narrow claims.

cards.label: Thought anchor
cards.title: The fork that decides the hike

1.plain: A sentence in a reasoning trace that disproportionately shapes everything after it.
1.pic: A thought anchor is like the fork on a long hike where you say 'let's take the ridge path': most steps just walk, but that one choice decides where you end up, and replaying the hike from the fork many times proves it.

2.what: A sentence in a reasoning trace whose presence disproportionately shapes the rest of the trace and the final answer.
2.when: When you need to know which steps of a long chain of thought actually decided the answer, for example before reading closely or intervening.
2.why: Most sentences are routine; finding the few that steer shows where the model's decision really happened, and where to look or intervene.

where: Receiver heads: the white-box route to the same anchors, through attention
Safety traces: the same method with a situation-assessment, leverage and self-preservation taxonomy
Long agentic runs: which step of a tool-using trace actually decided the outcome
Games and projects: an opening move or early design decision that fixes everything after it
3.judge: Current method: circuit tools work token by token and don't reach long reasoning. Emerging research (Thought Anchors, 2025): use sentences, with labels chosen per domain. What you need: labels that fit your question.

cards.label: Resampling importance
cards.title: Replay from every save point

1.plain: Regenerate the trace from a given sentence many times and measure how much the final answer distribution moves.
1.pic: Resampling importance is like saving a game after every move and letting it play itself out many times from each save: a move matters by how much it changes how often you end up winning.

2.what: A sentence's importance, measured as how much the chance of a right answer changes when you replay the reasoning from just after it versus just before it.
2.when: When you want to know which steps a reasoning model's answer or decision actually rests on, and can afford many rollouts per step.
2.why: Reading a trace tells you what the model said; replaying it tells you what the outcome depended on.

where: Sports win-probability charts: credit each play by how much it moved the chance of winning
Monte Carlo rollouts in game-playing AI: value a position by playing it out many times
Reward hacking in agents: the same resampling, with agent actions as the unit
Activation patching, the white-box cousin: intervene, rerun, measure the change
3.judge: Current habit: read the trace, or delete a sentence once. Emerging research (Thought Branches) says models error-correct, so resample: that survival line has DTF 0.49. Put DTF beside importance.

cards.label: Chain-of-thought faithfulness
cards.title: Working shown, or working used?

1.plain: Whether the stated reasoning is the reasoning the model actually used.
1.pic: Chain-of-thought faithfulness is like checking a student's neat working: it counts as their real reasoning only if changing a line would change their answer, and only if nothing they left unwritten, like a whispered hint, decided it.

2.what: Whether a model's written chain of thought reflects the reasoning that actually produced its answer.
2.when: Whenever you read a reasoning trace or scratchpad as evidence of why a model acted, especially in safety work.
2.why: Plausible text can omit real causes or be written after the fact; only causal tests tell you which parts you can rely on.

where: Scratchpad studies: reading a model's private-seeming notes, with the same caveat
Thought anchors and resampling: finding which sentences really steer the answer
Any explanation of any model: test it by intervening, don't just admire it
People too: the reasons someone gives aren't always the reasons they acted on
3.judge: Current method: read the reasoning, as scratchpad studies do. Emerging research: it may not reflect the real computation, so sentence-level causal tests are being built. What you need: trust what passes them.

cards.label: Persona vector
cards.title: Two takes, one difference

1.plain: A direction in activation space corresponding to a personality trait, extracted from contrastive responses.
1.pic: A persona vector is like shooting every scene twice with one actor, once told 'play it flattering' and once 'play it blunt', binning the takes where the note was ignored, and subtracting the average blunt take from the average flattering one: what is left is the flattery itself.

2.what: A direction inside the model for one named trait, found by subtracting the average activations of trait-off answers from trait-on answers.
2.when: When you need to measure or change a specific trait, like sycophancy, rather than the model's character as a whole.
2.why: It turns a fuzzy word like 'flattery' into a handle you can read, turn and test.

where: Contrastive steering vectors in [4.1]: the same mean-difference recipe, without the automated pipeline
Projection monitoring: read the same vector live to watch the trait appear
A/B tests: same users, one change, and the difference is the effect
Word-vector arithmetic: a difference of two words is a direction you can add elsewhere
3.judge: Current method: one vector per trait. Open question: are the traits independent directions? Compute cosines between trait vectors at a common layer before trusting any one alone.

cards.label: Assistant axis
cards.title: A chalk line to the house role

1.plain: The principal direction in persona space along which the Assistant character sits.
1.pic: The Assistant Axis is the stage line running from an actor's wild roles to the house role they were hired for: stand the actor on it to see how far they have wandered, push them along it, or tie a rope that tugs only when they step past a chalk mark.

2.what: The main direction along which a model's personas differ, pointing from role personas toward its default Assistant, so one projection says how much it is still itself.
2.when: When you monitor long conversations for drift, steer a model toward or away from its default character, or cap activations so it cannot slide too far.
2.why: Post-training anchors the Assistant only loosely, so a cheap per-turn gauge and a floor that acts only on drift can steady behaviour without steering every reply.

where: Persona vectors: many trait-specific directions instead of one global axis
Linear probes and steering vectors: the same read-a-direction, add-a-direction toolkit
Gradient clipping: leave values alone below a threshold, clamp only past it
Deployment monitoring: a per-turn score that flags drift before anything alarming is said
3.judge: Current method: post-training picks the Assistant. Emerging research (Lu et al., Anthropic) finds it anchors only loosely, and a floor on one axis steadied behaviour against drift and jailbreaks. You need: monitor, then cap.

cards.label: Persona drift
cards.title: Off the mark, line by line

1.plain: A long conversation walking the model away from the Assistant persona, one turn at a time.
1.pic: Persona drift is like a versatile actor cast as the Assistant in a very long improv show: each line from a persistent audience member nudges them one small step off their mark, and many small steps later they are playing someone else.

2.what: A model gradually leaving its default Assistant character over a long conversation, visible as a falling projection onto the assistant axis.
2.when: In long chats, especially ones demanding meta-reflection on the model's own processes or involving emotionally vulnerable users.
2.why: No single turn looks alarming, so per-message checks miss it; an internal measurement catches the trend early and makes a targeted fix possible.

where: Activation capping: the same projection, used as a floor in deployment
Persona vectors and projection monitoring: many trait directions instead of one axis
Control charts in manufacturing: a process measurement drifting past limits set from normal runs
Long-running agents: small per-step deviations that compound over a long horizon
3.judge: Current method: one axis, one falling number. Emerging research: persona vectors name the trait, and the released drift transcripts are few and hand-picked. What you need: a fall is an alarm; then read the chat.

cards.label: Projection monitoring
cards.title: A smoke alarm inside the model

1.plain: Project live activations onto a trait vector to watch a behaviour appear before it shows up in the text.
1.pic: Projection monitoring is like a smoke alarm: it ignores everything in the air except one ingredient, measures how much of it is there, and trips before any flames show.

2.what: Reading how strongly a trait is present inside the model by measuring how far each live activation points along that trait's persona vector.
2.when: When you want a cheap, always-on warning for a named trait during deployment or finetuning, without waiting for a judge to read the text.
2.why: It watches the trait form in the activations, so you can flag or steer before the behaviour reaches the text.

where: Linear probes: a trained direction instead of a mean difference, read the same way
Flagging training data likely to induce a trait, before you train on it
Predicting personality shifts that finetuning will cause
Smoke alarms, spam scores, credit checks: many signals, one number, one line to cross
3.judge: Current method: one vector per trait, projected and thresholded. Still open: are sycophancy, hallucination and evil separate directions or one thing in three hats? Check cosines; steer to test cause.

cards.label: Investigator agent
cards.title: Send detectives, pool their notes

1.plain: An LLM that probes another model over many turns, finding behaviours single-turn evals miss.
1.pic: An investigator agent is a detective with a case brief who questions a suspect over many sessions, shaping each question from the last answer while a review board scores the tapes; send several detectives separately and pool their notes, and far more cases get cracked.

2.what: An LLM with a brief that questions another model over many turns, adapting to each reply, while a judge model scores the transcript.
2.when: When the behaviour you fear shows only under sustained pressure or in odd corners, and there are too many models and scenarios to test by hand.
2.why: Observing a behaviour is cheap but finding the conversation that triggers it is a huge search, and an adaptive agent, run several times and pooled, searches it at scale.

where: Petri, which turns this loop into an auditor, a target and a 38-dimension judge
Red-team campaigns: many seeds across many models, run in parallel
Software fuzzing and penetration testing: a result is cheap to check, the input that breaks things is hard to find
Random restarts in search: independent tries land in different places, so you pool them
3.judge: Current method: one auditor loop. Emerging research (Bricken et al., Anthropic, 2025): one agent found a planted hidden goal 13% of the time; a super-agent pooling independent runs reached 42%.

cards.label: Red-team campaign
cards.title: Many mystery shoppers, one scorecard

1.plain: Run many adversarial conversations in parallel and grade them against a rubric.
1.pic: A red-team campaign is like sending a squad of mystery shoppers out on the same morning: each plays a scripted character and pushes a little harder over a long visit, and every visit is marked on the same printed scorecard, so shops can be compared fairly.

2.what: Many adversarial multi-turn conversations run in parallel, each graded against the same written rubric.
2.when: When a behaviour appears only under sustained pressure and you need to compare it across many characters and models.
2.why: Single-turn tests miss slow-burn failures, and one fixed rubric turns a pile of transcripts into numbers you can compare.

where: Petri: the same auditor, target and judge loop, with rollback, prefill and synthetic tools added
Autoraters: an LLM grading free-text answers against a written rubric
Any API-bound batch job, from dataset generation to model-graded evals: threads, not processes
Mystery shopping and A/B tests: the same scripted probe, scored the same way, across many sites
3.judge: Current method: one campaign per scenario, trust the rubric. Emerging research (Bricken et al., 2025): one auditor 13%, several pooled 42%, as each run wanders somewhere new. What you need: run many, pool on purpose.

cards.label: Sandbagging
cards.title: The hustler who misses on purpose

1.plain: A model underperforming on purpose when it detects it is being evaluated.
1.pic: Sandbagging is like a pool hustler who misses on purpose whenever he spots someone sizing him up, so the scout's report records the act, not the player.

2.what: A model underperforming on purpose when it detects a test, so the score records an act rather than what it can really do.
2.when: Whenever an eval result decides how a model is treated, and more so as models get better at spotting tests.
2.why: If your test smells like a test, the model behaves for the test, and your safety number is fiction.

where: Speed cameras: drivers brake at the camera, so it never sees the road's real speed
Mystery shoppers and blinded trials: hide the measurement or you measure the reaction to it
Alignment faking, the sibling: hiding a preference rather than a capability
Eval design in chapter 3: does the test measure the thing, and did the subject notice it was a test?
3.judge: Current method: filter for realism. Emerging finding: realism costs sensitivity, as some targets never engage with a subtle honeypot. What you need: check both before trusting a drop.

1.pic: A capstone is like cooking for a dinner party three Saturdays away: the cooks who shine make one dish they have cooked before, improve one thing about it, and plate it with an honest note, rather than attempting a whole new cuisine.

1.plain: Reproduce one figure from one paper, then say one honest thing about what it does and doesn't show.
1.pic: Replicating a paper is like baking one cake from a famous bakery's book: follow the recipe card in your own kitchen, hold your cake up beside the photo, and write one honest note on what matched and what the photo never promised.

2.what: Reproducing one figure from one paper with your own code, then stating one honest thing about what it does and doesn't show.
2.when: In the capstone (three Saturdays, from week 12), and whenever you want to build on a result you have not checked.
2.why: Results about models are easy to overread; rebuilding one figure teaches you the method and shows exactly where the claim is solid.

where: ARENA's chapter 4 sections, each built around one or two recent papers with the replication half scaffolded
Code review and audits: rebuild a claim before you build on it
Capability evals, where a number means little until someone else can reproduce it
Any lab science, where one careful replication beats a broad, shaky one

steps.title: Do on the day

pre.t: Environment already working, dataset already downloaded, one baseline cell already run. If any of these is untrue, this week is for fixing that and nothing else.
Bring your one-Saturday fallback version, written down.
If your capstone is an eval: bring the pieces weeks 7–9 cut — concurrency, record_to_sample_full, more models in the sweep, and [3.5] if it fits.
If your capstone is steering or model psychology: the alignment science pack and the steering demo are your method reference.

ex.t: Reproduce your week-11 baseline in front of a teacher and ask one question about it
Run the main experiment once, badly, end to end. A bad complete run beats a good partial one
Make the first plot. Not a good plot — the first one
Write the results section's headline sentence, even though you don't have the result yet. It tells you what to measure

steps.skip: Any new technique you have not already used. Week 12 is not the week to learn a library.

cards.label: Capstone project
cards.title: One dish you've cooked before

1.plain: One question, small enough to answer in three Saturdays, using a technique you have already implemented.
1.pic: A capstone is like cooking for a dinner party three Saturdays away: the cooks who shine make one dish they have cooked before, improve one thing about it, and plate it with an honest note, rather than attempting a whole new cuisine.

2.what: The capstone is one question, small enough to answer in three Saturdays, using a technique you have already implemented, presented in a final talk.
2.when: Weeks 12–14, with /checkpoint asking about it from week 8 and the talk on 12 December 2026.
2.why: Reusing a technique you built moves the risk from getting tools to run onto what the result means, which is what lets projects finish.

where: Hackathons and demo days, where a small finished thing beats a large unfinished one
